entries.title: CPD issues alert after armed robberies at dating app meetups in Princeton Park
entries.summary: <p>Chicago police are warning the public after three people were robbed at gunpoint in Princeton Park during meetings set up on dating apps, according to a bulletin released Wednesday.</p><p>The three reported robberies occurred in the 9200 block of South Harvard Avenue when someone was meeting another person from a dating app, and a man would demand their possessions at gunpoint, police said.</p><p>The most recent robberies occurred at 2:30 p.m. Oct. 18 and 5:30 p.m. Tuesday, police said. The suspect is described as a man about 6 feet tall with a slim build and light complexion who was wearing black clothing and a mask.</p><p>Anyone with information on the robberies can contact Chicago police at (312)747-8273.</p>
entries.author: Sun-Times Wire

entries.title: Man critically injured in Chatham shooting
entries.summary: <p>A man was shot multiple times in a shooting in the Chatham neighborhood Wednesday afternoon, according to Chicago police.</p><p>The man, 38, was in an alley near the 8100 block of South Drexel Avenue at 4:40 p.m. when he was shot in the arm, leg and torso, police said. He was taken to Trinity Hospital in critical condition.</p><p>No one is in custody. An investigation is ongoing, police said. </p>

entries.title: University of Chicago students rally with 'Jane Doe' in wake of sexual assault reports

Some teared up or hugged another person.</p><p>On Wednesday night, the students gathered to call on the University of Chicago to improve its sexual assault prevention and survivor support<a entries.title: Bulls rookie Caleb Wilson emitting young-Michael Jordan vibes with his play, talk
entries.summary: <p>It sounds like the good old days whenever he’s announced during introductions.</p><p>“From North Carolina …” Tim Sinclair blares.</p><p>Bulls fans of a certain age connect that school to one person, Michael Jordan. But in just a handful of games, Caleb Wilson has generated an excitement similar to the one those Bulls fans felt in 1984, when Jordan was just starting to get cooking on the West Side.</p><p>Not to put pressure on the kid — he’s 20 years old and looks younger — but the 16 points he scored in his first NBA game matched what His Airness scored in his. Five MVP Awards, 10 NBA scoring championships and six titles are right around the corner.</p><p>But here’s the thing: Wilson didn’t even give us the chance to anoint him as the Bulls’ next franchise player. He beat us to it, setting his sights on being the Rookie of the Year and striving to be the best player — ever.</p><p>Is there a rule against one city having two such players? Wilson would be happy to break it.</p><p>He doesn’t even think he’s putting undue pressure on himself. He believes he can do it.</p><p>“It’s just expectations for myself,” he said Wednesday. “If I stay healthy and I continue to do the work that I’m supposed to do, I feel like there’s no reason why I shouldn’t be a great player and hopefully Rookie of the Year.”</p><p>He certainly showed glimpses Monday in an otherwise forgettable night for the Bulls in Boston. During one stretch of the second quarter, Wilson beat Paul George one-on-one from the perimeter with a jab step and finished with a dunk, then beat George and Mitchell Robinson on the baseline with floater.</p><p>Those aren’t Wilson’s college contemporaries. Those are longtime NBA veterans. But Wilson has no symptoms of imposter syndrome.</p><p>“I definitely feel like I belong,” he said. “I feel like I’ve had great games, and, shoot, I’ve played against the best players and I’ve held my own and done well.”</p><p>That might look cocky in print, but it sounded nothing of the sort. When told that it appeared he was picking things up on the floor quickly, he responded with the most matter-of-fact “I told you so” ever spoken.</p><p>“Every game I learn something new, and I feel like every game I get better,” he said. “No matter what the stats say, I feel like I get better every single game. It’s so fun to see growth, and it’s so rapid for me.”</p><p>“We’re coaching him hard; he asked for that,” Bulls coach Tiago Splitter said. “He’s doing a lot of things that he’s not used to. He played at the four, big-man position in college, and he’s guarding [the Celtics’ Jayson] Tatum in a pick-and-roll. So there’s a lot of things for him to learn.”</p><p>One thing he already learned came from Jordan, who famously made up grudges and slights to motivate himself on the court. Wilson, a self-professed nice guy, said he needs to do something similar to conjure the venom required to compete in the NBA.</p><p>“When I go on the court, it’s hard to be, like, frustrated, but that’s when I play my best,” Wilson said. “So I just have to get that level of frustration and anger so I can play and be the best player I can be.”</p><p>MJ would be proud.</p><p>He also would be proud of the attention Wilson is drawing from the opposition. Wilson hasn’t even played a half-dozen games yet, but he appears to be at the top of scouting reports.</p><p>“Something that I’ve noticed, I’m usually getting the best defender every night,” Wilson said. “And I’m usually drawing two or three people every time I attack the paint. So just having that knowledge and knowing the gravity that I have in being able to create for others is something that I feel like I’ve really grown with lately.”</p><p>Wilson said his playmaking, not his scoring, has grown the fastest in his short time as a pro.</p><p>“I’ve missed a lot of shots I usually don’t miss lately,” he said. “It’s just conditioning, trying to adapt to the NBA game. But I’d say my playmaking is where I’m most happy that I’ve been growing offensively. Having that ability to make plays without turning the ball over is something that I’m really proud of. But I really hope that I can continue to grow there.”</p><p>Wilson already has faced some of the best players in the league, and more are on tap, including rematches with the Celtics and Knicks and his first look at LeBron James and the 76ers. He said sharing the court with such stars is surreal, which must be an understatement for a 20-year-old.</p><p>“I’m just a kid, so having an opportunity to play in Madison Square and TD Garden, that’s never going to not feel crazy to me,” Wilson said. “I’ve wanted to do that my whole life. So every time I go into an arena, I’m going to play to the best of my ability. I’m always going to do that.”</p><p>Sounds like a certain someone also from North Carolina.</p>
entries.author: Jeff Agrest

entries.title: Bulls offense is still a work in progress but ball security improving
entries.summary: <p>It’s been a point of emphasis since Tiago Splitter moved his stuff into the Bulls coaching office: Get Josh Giddey to play cleaner offense.</p><p>Last season, the veteran point guard handed out a career-high 9.1 assists per game but also established a career-high in turnovers with 3.6. His first year with the Bulls it was 2.9 turnovers per game. Coming from the Spurs culture like Splitter did, that’s a no-no.</p><p>So while the sample size is small so far, Giddey entered the game with the defending champions on Wednesday leading the team with 7.3 assists per game but just two turnovers per contest.</p><p>“Josh is also getting used to playing solo as bringing the ball (up),” Splitter said. “Before he had a lot of guys that can bring up the ball and create a bit more, but I think he’s doing a tremendous job of not turning the ball over as much. His assist-to-turnover ratio is way better. Yes, I want him to be more aggressive, yes, we’re not playing the way we want to yet. I think the process has been right.”</p><p>It may be right but not without problems.</p><p>The starters are still feeling each other out as far as shot selection and sharing the basketball, evident by the league-worst 40.6% shooting from the field and 23.8% from three-point range.</p><p>Numbers that Splitter feels will turn soon.</p><p>“Offensively, we’re getting the shots, most of the time, the shots we want,” Splitter said. “Unfortunately, we’re not making shots right now, which is part of the game. Sometimes you go through slumps, and we’ve got to start to make shots. But the process is right.”</p><p>Giddey was on the same page as his coach, feeling like it was just a matter of time.</p><p>“Every team coming out of training camp probably feels good about themselves, every team probably says they’re better than people think they’re going to be and blah, blah, blah,” Giddey said. “I believe in the group we have to start putting it together and we look good in stretches and we look horrible in stretches. So it’s just a matter of making those good stretches longer and those bad stretches shorter.”</p><p></p><p><b>Speed kills</b></p><p></p><p>Splitter was informed that almost 15% of the league was on the injury report before Wednesday’s games and did some self-scouting on how he would handle today’s style of play.</p><p>“I think the speed of the game is at a different level,” Splitter said. “If you want to ask me as a former player, the way I played was very slow, so I could not have played at this pace. Maybe as a back-up center. But yeah, the league is fast. Then you get to the games and the pressure, the high intensity is more than the summer, there’s an adjustment there, so you got to be careful how much you play your guys. If you’re not careful with the minutes and the loads, all that, it’s science like two plus two is four.”</p><p></p><p><b>Training room</b></p><p></p><p>The plan was to continue ramping up Nic Claxton (left hamstring) the next day and then take him on the East Coast swing to Boston, Philadelphia and New York. Does that mean the expected starting center will make his Bulls debut on that trip?</p><p>Not so fast.</p><p>“We’ll talk to our performance team, see where he’s at,” Splitter said. “He’s probably going to go with us because he’s almost there, just be part of what we’re doing as a group, even on the road. That’s the plan.”</p><p>As far as the two other injuries the group has been dealing with Patrick Williams (right adductor strain) and Tobe Awaka (left ankle sprain) remained out.</p>

entries.title: Charges pending for suspect accused of stabbing man at CTA Blue Line station
entries.summary: <p>A man was arrested after he allegedly stabbed another man on a CTA Blue Line station platform in West Town Wednesday evening, according to Chicago police.</p><p>The victim reportedly was in an argument with another man on the Division Blue Line platform at 8:25 p.m. when he was stabbed in the neck and back, police said. He was taken to Stroger Hospital in critical condition.</p><p>The suspect, who has not been identified, was later arrested, police said. </p>

entries.title: Bulls take two steps forward, one step back losing to the Knicks late
entries.summary: <p>There was no flinching from Caleb Wilson as he was trading blows with Landry Shamet down in the post. Not a second thought from Matas Buzelis when he came from behind on 290-pound center/left tackle Andre Drummond and blocked his shot.</p><p>Even Josh Giddey was all for some contact, posting up reserve guard Tyler Kolek and making him pay for trying to trade paint, hitting him with a floater.</p><p>The Bulls coaching staff – with the loudest voice being Tiago Splitter – had been pleading with the starters to start matching the physicality of opposing teams in a competitive fashion, and for the first three quarters on Wednesday, they finally seemed to get the message loud and clear.</p><p>The problem was there was a fourth quarter and that’s where the defending champions made their mark. Specifically, Finals MVP Jalen Brunson. Thanks to his 38 points (14 in the fourth), the Knicks outlasted the Bulls 133-127.</p><p>“We were focused for a longer period of time for the game, which is good, but the game still has 48 minutes,” Splitter said after the loss. “That fourth quarter wasn’t good enough. Of course they have great players. Brunson took over the game, and we tried a little bit of everything, but I think we competed for the most part.</p><p>“We got better (Wednesday).”</p><p>That the Bulls (1-4) did, and while no one was celebrating moral victories, it was undoubtedly another step forward in the rebuild.</p><p>“I told you I wasn’t going to take long,” Wilson, who finished with 20 points, said of his development from game to game. “Every game I just take the data, learn from it, watch games over, and it just happens for me. As long as I can see it, I’ll know what I need to do better, learn from it and it’s going to get better. That’s the good thing about me and us as a team, we’re young so we have a learning curve that we’re going to get to. It’s not like we’re a bunch of 30-year-olds. Once we get to that point, we’ll be great.”</p><p>“Great?” not there yet. Start with serviceable. Baby steps.</p><p>Considering New York was in town in front of a sold-out crowd at the United Center, however, steps that needed to be taken, and not only from Wilson.</p><p>The blowout loss in Boston on Monday felt like yet another rock bottom in the early part of this season, and not just because of the lack of physicality in that game, but the simple things like effort on rebounds. The Celtics beat the Bulls in a lot of ways, but 19 offensive rebounds didn’t go unnoticed.</p><p>Not that 16 offensive rebounds by the Knicks was major improvement, but there was at least an effort to find a body and hit a body. It was more bad bounces than bad technique. That can be lived with.</p><p>“You saw (Splitter’s) team in Portland (last season), they were good at rebounding, and we’ve got to do it more,” Giddey said. “It sounds so simple but it’s not as simple as it looks. It just kills a team’s spirit when you consistently offensive rebound, so we’ve got to look at it that way and try to get better at it.”</p><p>The good news is the rebounding and physicality will continue being tested, as the Bulls go back to Boston on Friday, play in Philadelphia on Monday, and a rematch with the Knicks next week.</p><p>“For sure technique and communication, also just covering for each other, sacrificing for each other to make tough plays,” Wilson said of the ongoing progress. “I feel like if we continue learning how to play with one another it will lead to a lot better things happening.”</p>

entries.title: Motorcyclist killed, passenger critically injured in crash with SUV in Woodlawn
entries.summary: <p>A 21-year-old man driving a motorcycle was killed and his passenger critically injured when an SUV crashed into them while turning Wednesday night in Woodlawn on the South Side. </p><p>Around 9:10 p.m., a silver SUV was trying to turn left onto 61st Street when it slammed into a motorcycle going north on Cottage Grove Avenue, Chicago police said. </p><p>The motorcycle driver, a 21-year-old man, was taken to the University of Chicago Medical Center where he died, police said. </p><p>A passenger on the motorcycle, a 24-year-old man, was also taken to the University of Chicago where he was in critical condition, officials said. </p><p>The SUV driver was given a citation. </p>

entries.title: Supreme Court case highlights irrationality of home distilling ban
entries.summary: <p>Years ago, I bought a contraption designed to separate and concentrate the most volatile components of a liquid mixture. I would tell you what I did with it, but I don't want to implicate myself in a federal felony.</p><p>Since 1868, it has been <a class="Link" href="https://www.law.cornell.edu/uscode/text/26/5178" target="_blank" >illegal</a> for Americans to locate a "distilled spirits plant" in "any dwelling place," an offense <a class="Link" href="https://www.law.cornell.edu/uscode/text/26/5601" target="_blank" >punishable</a> by a maximum $10,000 fine and up to five years in prison. The federal ban on home distilling is at the center of a <a class="Link" href="https://www.supremecourt.gov/docket/docketfiles/html/public/26-204.html" target="_blank" >case</a> that the Supreme Court recently <a class="Link" href="https://reason.com/2026/10/20/trump-administration-urges-scotus-to-uphold-federal-ban-on-distilling-liquor-at-home/" target="_blank" >agreed</a> to hear, which raises a specific constitutional issue but also highlights the absurdity of treating this hobby as a crime.</p><p>That policy, the U.S. Court of Appeals for the 5th Circuit <a class="Link" href="https://reason.com/2026/05/13/a-circuit-split-gives-scotus-an-opportunity-to-overturn-a-federal-law-that-makes-home-distilling-a-felony/" target="_blank" >ruled</a> in April, cannot be justified as an exercise of the federal government's tax power. To the contrary, Judge Edith Jones said in the court's <a class="Link" href="https://www.ca5.uscourts.gov/opinions/pub/24/24-10760-CV0.pdf" target="_blank" >opinion</a>, the ban is "an anti-revenue provision that prevents distilled spirits from coming into existence," meaning its effect is "to reduce revenue instead of raising it."</p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-floatRight><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-060000" name="module-060000"></a> <div class="RichTextSidebarModule-title">Columnist </div> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody"><h2>Columnists</h2></div> </div><p>Nor is the provision consistent with "the Supreme Court's explanation of how the federal power of taxation works," Jones wrote. When Congress imposes a tax, the court <a class="Link" href="https://tile.loc.gov/storage-services/service/ll/usrep/usrep567/usrep567519/usrep567519.pdf" target="_blank" >explained</a> in 2012, it "leaves an individual with a lawful choice to do or not do a certain act, so long as he is willing to pay a tax levied on that choice." But in this case, Jones noted, would-be home distillers "have only the choice not to do as they wish or risk fines and imprisonment."</p><p>The government argued that the ban helps collect liquor taxes by prohibiting a form of production that is difficult to detect. But "Congress cannot prohibit intrastate activity solely because it might produce products hard to tax," Jones said. If it could, she warned, there would be "no limit whatsoever" to its tax power.</p><p>Under the government's logic, Jones noted, "Congress may criminalize nearly any at-home conduct only because it has the possibility of concealing taxable activity. Home-based businesses may be forbidden. Remote work may be deemed a crime."</p><p>The Trump administration, which wants the Supreme Court to overturn the 5th Circuit's decision, <a class="Link" href="https://www.supremecourt.gov/DocketPDF/26/26-204/419168/20260814181724147_McNutt_cert_petition.pdf" target="_blank" >argues</a> that threatening to imprison home distillers is a "necessary and proper" safeguard against tax evasion. But whatever your take on the constitutional question, that policy is morally indefensible, haphazardly enforced and inconsistent with the federal government's treatment of wine and beer.</p><p>The lead plaintiff in this case is Scott McNutt, a member of the <a class="Link" href="https://hobbydistillersassociation.com/" target="_blank" >Hobby Distillers Association</a>. In 2014, McNutt received a "Notice of Potential Civil and Criminal Liability" from the Treasury Department, which said it had reason to believe he "may have purchased a still capable of producing alcohol and/or equipment and materials that may be used in the manufacture of a still."</p><p>The notice warned that "federal law provides no exemptions for the production of distilled spirits for personal or family use." It added that "unlawful production of distilled spirits is a criminal offense," which it erroneously claimed was "punishable by a fine of up to $500,000" as well as "imprisonment for not more than 5 years."</p><p>Meanwhile, online retailers such as Amazon <a class="Link" href="https://www.amazon.com/s?k=home+still&crid=3IGTBXAJMQFW3&sprefix=home+still%2Caps%2C205&tag=reasonmagazinea-20&ref=nb_sb_noss_1" target="_blank" >sell</a> a wide variety of home stills, many of which are explicitly <a class="Link" href="https://www.amazon.com/dp/B0F228DJS1/ref=nosim?tag=reasonmagazinea-20" target="_blank" >advertised</a> as appliances designed to produce alcoholic beverages such as vodka, gin, brandy and whiskey. Customers could be forgiven for assuming that's legal, especially since federal law has long permitted home <a class="Link" href="https://www.law.cornell.edu/cfr/text/27/24.75" target="_blank" >wine</a> and <a class="Link" href="https://www.congress.gov/95/statute/STATUTE-92/STATUTE-92-Pg1255.pdf" target="_blank" >beer</a> production "for personal or family use."</p><p>McNutt's lawyers <a class="Link" href="https://www.supremecourt.gov/DocketPDF/26/26-204/424681/20260917144108453_26-204%20Brief%20for%20Respondents.pdf" target="_blank" >say</a> he "owns a still that he has used to lawfully distill fuel alcohol and seeks to 'tinker around' with beverage spirits." Another plaintiff, Thomas Cowdrey, "likewise seeks to experiment in creating new beverage spirits, including 'apple pie vodka,' for which he has developed a recipe."</p><p>Because of a law Congress enacted 158 years ago, McNutt and Cowdrey would be felons if they acted on those desires. It might be time to rethink that policy.</p><p><i>Jacob Sullum is a senior editor at Reason magazine.</i></p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-center><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-530000" name="module-530000"></a> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody">Send letters to <a class="Link" href="mailto:letters@suntimes.com" target="_blank" >letters@suntimes.com</a>. More about <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/submitting-opinion-and-letters" >how to submit here</a>.</div> </div><p></p>

entries.title: Dear Abby: Woman with great life dreams of doom
entries.summary: <p><b>DEAR ABBY:</b> Let me start off by saying I have a great life, a good job, a loving boyfriend and family I adore. I'm a 42-year-old woman with grown children and grandkids. In the past, I struggled with low self-esteem and now choose to keep to myself.</p><p>My life with my boyfriend of seven years has helped me to be more open and has boosted my self-worth. With him, I don't have to hold back about what I am truly feeling inside. However, for the past couple of years, I have been wishing to be in a car accident or get injured in some way just to feel pain. I often see accidents on the highway and can't help thinking "that should have been me."</p><p>I don't want to kill myself or wish harm on others, but I just can't get this feeling out of my head. I don't want to talk about it with my boyfriend because I'm afraid he'll think I might harm myself and would worry. I have considered counseling, but I'm afraid I'll be prescribed depression medication or, worse, be hospitalized.</p><p>I'm sure this isn't normal, but some part of me hopes I just might be normal and that there are others who think like me. Abby, I'm not sure what I am asking for ... maybe reassurance that I am not crazy? — <i>LOW SELF-WORTH IN TEXAS</i></p><p><b>DEAR LOW SELF-WORTH:</b> Allow me to be the first person to reassure you that you are not crazy. (The second should be a licensed mental health professional.) You are not alone in your feelings. You have a lot of company.</p><p>When people have suffered with self-esteem issues for a long time, sometimes on a subconscious level they begin to feel they deserve any unhappiness that comes their way. When they finally find happiness in their lives, they feel they should be punished for it. That may be what's going on with you.</p><p>As to your worry about being locked up if you discuss this with a mental health professional, that's not true. Many people who know they need to talk to someone harbor the same fear that you have. I hope you will find a way to talk to someone about your feelings, because I believe they can be overcome — not because you now have a wonderful boyfriend, but because you're stronger and more capable of growth than you think.</p><p><b>DEAR ABBY:</b> Would it be inappropriate to send a sympathy card to a man who lost his wife a couple of months ago? I love this man; we have a history. We are now in our 60s. We met when we were in our 30s. Please advise. — <i>LONELY</i></p><p><b>DEAR LONELY:</b> It would be brazen of you to try to rekindle a romantic spark in this way, but if you can keep your message merely friendly and sympathetic, it should be fine. I advise against making any further gestures, however. If he ever decides he's ready to start a new chapter with you, he needs to be the one to initiate that.</p><p><i>Dear Abby is written by Abigail Van Buren. For nearly four decades, Jeanne Phillips penned this column, which was founded in 1956 by her mother, Pauline Phillips. Contact Dear Abby at www.DearAbby.com or P.O. Box 270135, Kansas City, MO 64127.</i></p>
entries.author: Abigail Van Buren

entries.title: Trump seems determined to help Republicans lose midterm elections
entries.summary: <p>Despite how ubiquitous, prolix and attention-seeking he is, sometimes it’s still hard to know what makes President Donald Trump do the things he does.</p><p>Why, for example, is he so fixated on “acquiring” <a class="Link" href="https://www.whitehouse.gov/briefings-statements/2026/09/agreement-between-the-government-of-the-united-states-of-america-and-the-government-of-the-kingdom-of-denmark-together-with-the-government-of-greenland-to-amend-and-supplement-the-agreement-of-27-apri/" target="_blank" >places like Greenland</a>? Why is he obsessed with renaming things and changing the maps? Shouldn’t he be too busy presidenting to care about whatever <a class="Link" href="https://truthsocial.com/@realDonaldTrump/posts/117504266048722465" target="_blank" >Bill Maher said about him</a>? And what the hell is with all the butt talk lately?</p><p>We’ll leave that to psychiatrists to solve. But most bizarre and baffling of all, Trump has seemed determined to help Republicans lose their midterm elections all over the country — and it’s anyone’s guess as to why.</p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-floatRight><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-390000" name="module-390000"></a> <div class="RichTextSidebarModule-title">Columnist </div> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody"><h2>Columnists</h2></div> </div><p>Maybe it’s because he’s not on the ballot. Maybe he secretly misses sparring with Democrats while Republicans have had total control of Congress. Maybe he’s just bored. Who knows?</p><p>Thankfully, Trump’s inner workings will likely remain a mystery. But sometimes, he just comes out and tells us what he’s thinking. It’s in these moments, when he says the quiet part out loud, that we often learn the most about him.</p><p>Over the weekend, with just over a week to go before elections, Trump was on the stump in places Republicans should be doing much better in. But again, because of his inexplicable decisions — to prosecute a war no one wanted in an election year, to intentionally throw grenades into safe Republican primaries, to say things like “<a class="Link" href="https://www.independent.co.uk/news/world/americas/us-politics/trump-vance-economy-affordability-voters-b3070641.html" target="_blank" >affordability is a hoax</a>” — his rambling and untethered rallies have made for some odd final moments.</p><p>During a Georgia rally, he went on a long riff that can only be described as political suicide — or is it homicide? Either way, it was nuts.</p><p>“The United States oil and gas business is making hundreds of billions of dollars,” <a class="Link" href="https://www.cbsnews.com/news/trump-oil-gas-stocks-gain-millions-iran-war-democratic-report-finds/" target="_blank" >he crowed</a>.</p><p>And then he told on himself.</p><p>“But my people said, 'Please don’t mention that, sir.' Because people are paying a little higher. ... No, I could just see the fake headlines. 'President Trump is talking about all the money they’re making while the people are suffering at the pump. That’ll be the headline. But I said, 'I don’t give a damn. I’m gonna say it: We’re making a freaking fortune.'"</p><p>Now, this was revealing in two ways. There would've been a thought among politicos that maybe his inner circle wasn’t telling him how impolitic and imprudent it was to diminish the pain Americans are feeling, to call that pain a hoax and to brag about inflation, the war, tariffs and how much oil companies have made.</p><p>After all, also over the weekend, Trump told a conservative news outlet that his approval is in the 60s. <a class="Link" href="https://www.yahoo.com/news/politics/articles/donald-trump-says-polls-fake-170114668.html" target="_blank" >It is not</a>. It’s about 30 points south of that.</p><p>But clearly, that wasn’t the case. He was told, and he didn’t care.</p><p>That’s the second revelation. He doesn’t care who this messaging — and one has to assume the policies behind them — hurt. That goes for American voters as well as Republican candidates.</p><p>This shouldn’t be a surprise to anyone who’s been paying attention. Trump’s priorities as president seem to be lining his own pockets and building monuments to himself.</p><p>But to hear him say it so clearly, 10 days before a midterm election, admittedly against the advice of his team, is pretty astonishing.</p><p>“I don’t care about your pain” — a reverse Clinton — certainly isn’t a strategy we’ve seen work … ever, anywhere. And it’s one helluva closing argument.</p><p>He might not care that his policies have hurt you. But you do. He might not be worried about the future. But you are. He might not care, for whatever reason, about these elections. But you should.</p><p><i>S.E. Cupp is the host of “S.E. Cupp Unfiltered” on CNN.</i></p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-center><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-eb0000" name="module-eb0000"></a> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody">Send letters to <a class="Link" href="mailto:letters@suntimes.com" target="_blank" >letters@suntimes.com</a>. More about <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/submitting-opinion-and-letters" >how to submit here</a>.</div> </div><p></p>

entries.title: In pursuing stories on the 'evangelical industrial complex,' Julie Roys sees journalism as a 'sacred calling'
entries.summary: <p>For a country that over the last 25 years has come to associate religious scandal with the Catholic church, Julie Roys is here to tell us something:</p><p>Other Christian churches also have their fair share of failings, whether involving sexual abuse, financial misconduct or some other hypocrisy running counter to Jesus’ teachings.</p><p>The proof is Roys' news web site called Roys Report that regularly publishes articles — many investigative in nature — on troubles in evangelical Christian congregations and organizations.</p><p>“There are wonderful pastors out there,” Roys said. “But there are a lot of bad ones, too.”</p><p>“It’s not just a few bad apples — it’s a system.”</p><p>One of her news site’s recent journalistic focal points has been Wheaton College, an evangelical school in the far west suburbs that’s sometimes referred to as the “Harvard of Christian colleges.”</p><p>Roys Report published a series of blistering stories this year about Dennis Massaro, a former Wheaton administrator who has been accused of sexually abusing male students years ago, and who was at the school when Roys was an undergraduate in the 1980s.</p><p>“Massaro, who served as the director of Wheaton’s Office of Christian Outreach for 19 years, was dismissed by Wheaton in 1998,” Roys recently wrote. “But two Wheaton administrations — under both Presidents Duane Litfin and Philip Ryken — kept Massaro’s alleged criminal sexual assault hidden until 2024.”</p><p>“Wheaton’s silence... enabled Massaro to continue serving in church ministries for decades, giving him access to unsuspecting young men,” according to another story by Roys.</p><p>Massaro has not been charged with a crime and could not be reached for comment.</p><p>Wheaton’s president since 2010, Ryken has come under additional scrutiny as Roys’ web site reported he’d once been censured by the Presbyterian Church in America for allegedly “limiting the investigation into” another minister’s alleged sexual misconduct “and withholding information about the abuse.”</p><p>A Wheaton spokesman said that Ryken “stood with the elders and victims before members of the congregation and others to ask for and receive forgiveness by apologizing publicly for failing to take additional necessary steps of pastoral oversight when he first learned of the abuse.”</p><div class="Enhancement" class="Figure-credit"><p>Sun-Times file, Wheaton College</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>The school also released a statement about Massaro, saying “we are deeply sorry for Dennis Massaro’s sexual abuse of students in the 1990s — conduct for which he was forced to resign. We have also apologized for not enforcing more effectively his restriction from campus and for the pain experienced over the ensuing years by the victims and his family.”</p><p>But that subject is just the tip of the ecclesiastical iceberg, with Roys Report recently writing unrelated stories about a “young Baptist missionary with a large TikTok following” who has been accused of molesting boys in Haiti, an Oklahoma youth pastor facing criminal charges for allegedly abusing “teenage girls under his care” and a “popular Christian writer” confessing to “a sinful affair with a married woman.”</p><h3>Serving the ideal of truth</h3><p>Roys, 61, said the intent of her site’s news stories isn’t to tear down faith or organized religion, but rather to serve a shared ideal at the core of journalism and Christianity: truth.</p><p>“Ironically, my Intro to Journalism professor at Wheaton College, the late Paul Fromer, taught me that journalism was a sacred calling to pursue and report the truth,” Roys said. Fromer also edited books by the college's most famous graduate, the late evangelist Billy Graham. “He pointed to the Gospel writer Luke as the first journalist. Luke was not a first-hand witness to the events he documented.”</p><p>“Instead, he interviewed the first-hand witnesses and ‘carefully investigated everything from the beginning,’ so he might ‘write an orderly account... that you may know the certainty of the things you have been taught.’ This understanding has been foundational for me and guided my work.”</p><p>Beyond that, there is a strong element of advocacy with Roys Report — harnessing that truth to reform and cleanse. Consider the catchphrase for Roys Report, a nonprofit that relies on donations: “Reporting the Truth. Restoring the Church.”</p><p>Roys said a “major donor noted a couple years ago that we were doing a great job reporting the truth, but challenged us to do more to restore the church. We host a Restore Conference for survivors of church hurt and those concerned about church reform about once every 18 months to two years. But other than that, we haven't had the resources to do much more.”</p><p>“This donor gave us a significant gift to launch <i>restoringthechurch.com...</i> that will provide resources for survivors to heal, for church leaders to cultivate healthy faith communities, and for donors to follow best practices to ensure their money is used wisely. I’m very excited about launching this new initiative to provide solutions to the problems our reporting exposes.”</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" enormity of the problem in the church and especially evangelicalism. Now I recognize that it's not just a few bad apples but systemic rot fueled by money, power and unchristian leadership models. And, just like the Protestant Reformation took 130 years to undo church abuses, it will likely take at least several decades of reporting to bring about meaningful church reform.”</p><p>Roys said her news site — which also now includes a YouTube channel — reports many stories “that Christian media is afraid to touch and that secular media often ignores.”</p><h3>Roys Report’s global reach</h3><p>While Roys lives in West Chicago, and her web site is based locally, her coverage extends around the country and, around the globe.</p><p>A married mother of adult children who’s also a grandmother, Roys was partly raised internationally. Her parents were Christian missionaries. “I was born overseas, in Zimbabwe, in what at the time was Southern Rhodesia,” Roys said.</p><p>It was common that locals would die from very treatable ailments because there simply weren’t enough physicians, medical facilities and drugs. Her father, a doctor, was a “medical missionary” who not only helped treat Africans with medical needs, he trained others on certain procedures. Roys’ mother would be “his scrub nurse.”</p><p>Roys’ father was part of the Brethren in Christ denomination, whose “preaching and teaching is shaped by four emphases within the wider Christian community: Anabaptism, Pietism, Wesleyanism and Evangelicalism,” according to a church web site.</p><p>“This Anabaptist strain within our Church’s ‘theological DNA’ shows itself most particularly in our emphases on the community of faith, serving compassionately, living simply and pursuing peace.”</p><p>Roys’ mother was Wesleyan, and the “Wesleyan movement in America — also known as the Holiness movement — emphasized conversion as a conscious acceptance of God, as well as the empowerment of the Holy Spirit and daily growth in holiness,” according to the Brethren in Christ web page.</p><div both sides of my family there was this really strong” belief “that Christians should behave,” Roys said. “That was just built into me.”</p><p>While still young, her family moved back to the U.S. She was mostly in Pennsylvania, until attending Wheaton College where she worked at the student newspaper. She earned a master’s degree in broadcast journalism from Northwestern University.</p><p>Later, she worked for mainstream media outlets, and was a national host for Moody Radio — part of the Moody Bible Institute, an evangelical college based in Chicago and founded in the late 1800s by pioneering evangelist and publisher Dwight L. Moody.</p><p>Roys also maintained a personal blog and in 2018 “published a series of articles on her web site, exposing corruption and mission drift at the Moody Bible Institute," according to her official biography.</p><p>“This led to the exit of three top officers at Moody. It also ended Julie’s relationship with Moody and changed the focus of Julie’s web site — from a blog offering cultural commentary to an independent Christian media outlet exposing corruption, abuse and what’s been termed the 'evangelical industrial complex.'"</p><h3>At first, a local focus</h3><h3></h3><p>Roys Report’s coverage was initially quite local — with a series of stories focusing on class="Figure-credit"><p>Pat Nabong / Sun-Times</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>Roys said she stands by the facts of the reporting.</p><p>In 2019 Roys Report’s revenue was around $137,000. In the fiscal year that just ended, it was more than $600,000. The organization began with just Roys and now has four full-time employees, including former Christianity Today writer and editor Daniel Silliman. Roys Report has had more than 12 million views on the site so far this year.</p><p>Roys Report stories, and impact, have expanded across the country. And Roys said her news site’s coverage was a factor in numerous actions, including:<br></p><ul class="rte2-style-ul" id="rte-d1d8bdc2-cf28-11f1-bcd2-cd6fb8eb08dc"><li>The Ravi Zacharias International Ministries commissioning a report that determined the group’s namesake, a well-known evangelist who died in 2020, sexually and spiritually abused women.<br></li><li>The International House of Prayer in Kansas City parting ways with founder Mike Bickle after church officials say they “learned of allegations and testimonies of sexual abuse and manipulation.”<br></li><li>Truett McConnell University, a Baptist college in Georgia, firing the school’s president in 2025 over his handling of sexual misconduct accusations against an administrator.</li></ul><p>The college president, Emir Caner, sued the school this year saying he was wrongly fired, according to a Washington Post story that cited Roys Report’s reporting.</p><p>The Guardian also cited Roys Report earlier this year in its reporting on Michael Tait, ex-frontman of the Nashville-based Christian rock band Newsboys who has been accused of drug use and “predatory” sexual behavior dating back decades.</p><p>Newsboys and affiliates subsequently sued Roys Report in federal court for defamation, but Roys stood by the articles, saying in April: “The threat of this kind of ungodly retaliation is precisely why the truth about Michael Tait and the Newsboys remained buried for so long.”</p><p>“But The Roys Report has never refused, and will never refuse, to report a story due to fear. Our coverage was carefully reported, based on multiple independent sources and corroborated before publication.”</p><p>A number of other defendants were named in the suit, which alleged there was a conspiracy in which news stories were fueled by “competitors” in the lucrative Christian music business “with anti-competitive motives.”</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div / AP Photo</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>Roys Report’s stories also often expose problems in sprawling evangelical congregations.</p><p>Locally, perhaps the best-known megachurch is Willow Creek Community Church, based in South Barrington and founded decades ago by Bill Hybels. As <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/the-watchdogs/2026/09/28/willow-creek-community-church-south-barrington-evangelical-megachurch-congregation-sexual-abuse-cars-ministry" target="_blank" >the Chicago Sun-Times recently reported</a>, a former member recently sued Willow Creek saying she was sexually abused years earlier, as a teen, by a man employed by one of the church ministries.</p><p>Speaking generally, Roys said such venues — with their stages, auditorium seating and emphasis on entertainment-style services — too often seem to attract “narcissist” pastors who crave the limelight rather than embody the humility that Christianity emphasizes.</p><p>Too many ministers are “manipulating scriptures for their own selfish ends,” and too many faith groups have essentially become businesses, Roys said.</p><h3>Roys’ ‘house church’</h3><p>“I have a real tough time with a lot of churches,” Roys said, with her reporting making it difficult at times to feed her own spiritual needs. “I know too much.”</p><p>But she said she has found a “house church” in the suburbs that she’s part of now and includes a number of people who meet in someone’s home.</p><p>“We don’t have a pastor but we have plenty of people who are shepherds,” Roys said. “I wouldn’t know where my faith would be without them.”</p><p>Since the initial Roys Report articles, “it’s been nonstop story after story,” Roys said. “We’re filling this niche... we believe that truth is restorative.”</p><p>Even so, Roys Report wasn’t something Roys plotted out, or at first wanted to do. “I don’t feel like I volunteered, I feel like I got drafted,” she said. Given the content of much of the coverage, “it’s been awful,” but in telling the truth, and often making an impact, “it’s also wonderful.”</p><div class="RelatedList Enhancement" data-module data-align-center> <div class="RelatedList-title">Related</div> <ul class="RelatedList-items"> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/the-watchdogs/2026/09/28/willow-creek-community-church-south-barrington-evangelical-megachurch-congregation-sexual-abuse-cars-ministry" target="_blank" >Woman alleges in new lawsuit she was sexually abused as a teen in 1990s at the Willow Creek megachurch</a> </li> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/the-watchdogs/2025/11/24/chapelstreet-church-geneva-brian-coffey-lawsuit-child-sexual-abuse-baptist-evangelical" target="_blank" >Did suburban megachurch pastor ever report suspected child sexual abuse by a youth leader to authorities?</a> </li> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/the-watchdogs/2025/11/10/chapelstreet-church-geneva-evangelical-sexual-abuse-baptist-denomination" target="_blank" >Suburban megachurch sued over alleged sexual abuse by youth leader; pastor accused of cover-up</a> </li> </ul> </div> <p></p>

" srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/1270a2f/2147483647/strip/true/crop/8192x4598+0+433/resize/490x275!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F30%2F27%2F0819dd814d26b2806a648e24c808%2Fcarriecoon-2611060470.jpg 1x,https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/56b067b/2147483647/strip/true/crop/8192x4598+0+433/resize/980x550!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F30%2F27%2F0819dd814d26b2806a648e24c808%2Fcarriecoon-2611060470.jpg 2x" width="490" height="275" data-src="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/1270a2f/2147483647/strip/true/crop/8192x4598+0+433/resize/490x275!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F30%2F27%2F0819dd814d26b2806a648e24c808%2Fcarriecoon-2611060470.jpg" data-lazy-load="true" src="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" > </picture> <div class="Figure-content"><figcaption class="Figure-caption"><p>Carrie Coon speaks at Music Box Theatre after accepting the Artistic Achievement Award, granted by the Chicago International Film Festival. </p></figcaption><span class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Manuel Martinez/WBEZ</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>Illustrated by her latest film role in Guy Nattiv’s “The Liberation,” as a Holocaust survivor who joins a cult, Coon has a knack for playing complex women across theater stages (“<a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/theater/2025/08/20/carrie-coon-broadway-bug-tracy-letts-steppenwolf-theatre" >Bug</a>," “Who’s Afraid of Virginia Woolf”), TV roles (“The Leftovers,” <a class="Link" href="https://www.wbez.org/movies-tv/white-lotus-carrie-coon-steppenwolf-theatre" ><u>“White Lotus”</u></a>) and movies. Still, despite her status as one of the most critically acclaimed working actors today, Coon, 45, still has to fight for major film roles.</p><p>In 2025, the number of women and girls leading the top films fell from 55% to 39% — hitting a seven-year low, <a class="Link" href="https://deadline.com/2026/02/women-film-roles-seven-year-low-usc-annenberg-study-1236706727/" target="_blank" ><u>according to a University of Southern California study</u></a>. Even “The Liberation,” due in January, faced financial challenges and took more than a decade to make.</p><p>“It's hard to get money for films about complicated women,” Coon said before the ceremony, which preceded a screening of the film. “For a leading role like this to come my way is very rare. I’m not typically in that conversation.”</p><h3>A transformative film role</h3><p>Viewers at this moment may be most familiar with Coon for her role as the social-climbing matriarch Bertha Russell in “The Gilded Age,” which returns for season four on Sunday. (The cast will also release “Voices of the Gilded Age: The Christmas Album,” on Nov. 6.)<b> </b>Coon said fans can expect to see a different side of character, as she grapples with loneliness amid a rocky marriage.</p><p>She filmed the new season of the HBO show after wrapping work as Laurie Duffy in season three of “The White Lotus,” an opportunity she considered crucial for the “longevity of her career” as a woman in her 40s.</p><p>Coon, who is also known for dynamic theater roles, hopes she can continue to portray multifaceted women in future productions. In “The Liberation,” Coon’s character, Rita Cooper, is based on Nattiv’s real-life grandmother. Coon stars alongside her husband, actor and playwright Tracy Letts, who portrays her spouse in the film, as well as Bella Ramsey (“The Last of Us”) and Odessa Young (“Springsteen: Deliver Me from Nowhere”), who play their daughters. Lily James (“Downton Abbey”) takes on the role of the alluring cult leader, Ricki King.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure-content"><figcaption class="Figure-caption"><p>In Guy Nattiv’s “The Liberation,” Carrie Coon portrays Rita Cooper, who undergoes both an emotional and physical transformation. </p></figcaption><span class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Courtesy of Bleecker Street</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>Coon prepared for the role by watching testimonials from Holocaust survivors, including those recorded by Nattiv’s grandmother for the Yad Vashem Holocaust Remembrance Center. And she said teaming up with her real-life husband was ideal, not only because of the built-in intimacy, but Letts’ strength as a supporting character.</p><p>“Tracy is not the kind of actor who is going to take all the air out of a room,” said Coon, who, like Letts, is a member of Steppenwolf Theatre’s ensemble. “I knew I was getting a great ensemble player who was there to make me look as good as I could look in any scene.”</p><p>Coon conveys Cooper’s depression — and repression — as she abandons her family and bank job for a more “spiritual” life under King’s tutelage. Though she finds relief from the trauma of her past, she winds up trading one form of imprisonment for another.</p><p>But Coon said she can relate to Cooper’s desire to relinquish control.</p><p>“As a woman who's a wife and a mother who makes decisions all day, I totally understand,” she said. “I think Guy has done a really good job humanizing every decision [Cooper] makes that takes her down this path.”</p><p>The character undergoes both an emotional and physical transformation in the role, which required Coon to lose some weight.</p><p>“So often people don't experience frailty or weakness in my work, and so it was nice for me to get to explore that part of myself,” she said. “We cut my hair, which men get Oscars for, but that was fun for me. It almost feels like two different characters.”</p><h3>A rocky path to the screen</h3><p>Nattiv had a bumpy journey getting “The Liberation” to the big screen. Before he secured a distribution deal with Bleecker Street, studios tried to persuade him to do everything from removing the Holocaust narrative to changing the non-linear structure of the film.</p><p>Coon chalked those hurdles up to the challenging landscape for female-led films in the U.S. She lamented the lack of representation, especially for women of color, in movies receiving awards buzz this year.</p><p>“So often the films that are in consideration for these awards have the same five or six movie stars,” she said. “They're great, and we want to see them. And yet, I wish there was more room for other people.”</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="AnchorLink" in the movie as Rita Cooper alongside her husband, actor and playwright Tracy Letts.</p></figcaption><span class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Manuel Martinez/WBEZ</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>Coon said she also tries to seek out women directors, but they are facing their own struggles. In 2025, only about 10% of films were directed by women, setting progress back to 2018 levels, according to a <a class="Link" href="https://socialsciences.ucla.edu/wp-content/uploads/2026/03/UCLA-Hollywood-Diversity-Report-2026-Theatrical-Film-3-12-2026.pdf" target="_blank" ><u>Hollywood Diversity report</u></a> by the University of California, Los Angeles. And this year, Venice Film Festival jury president Maggie Gyllenhaal <a class="Link" href="https://deadline.com/2026/09/venice-maggie-gyllenhaal-empathy-politics-charged-women-1237065247/" target="_blank" ><u>made headlines</u></a> when she spoke out about the lack of female directors in the main competition.</p><p>“I work with all these male auteurs,” Coon said during a Q&A following “The Liberation” screening at Music Box Theatre. “The hard truth is that women don't get a chance. Even when they make a good movie, they rarely get a chance to make another one.”</p><p>Fans can see Coon in two forthcoming movies by women directors: “Honeymoon/Funeral,” a romantic comedy by Nahnatchka Khan, and “Daddy Daughter Dance,” a comedy shot in Chicago by Kelly O’Sullivan, along with her <a class="Link" href="https://www.wbez.org/theater-stages/2024/06/11/ghostlight-movie-keith-kupferer-chicago-theater-actors" target="_blank" ><u>filmmaking partner,</u></a> Alex Thompson.</p><p>Besides telling stories about complicated women, Coon is also interested in something else women aren’t typically asked to do: push their bodies to new limits. It could be anything from kicking butt in an action movie or training to portray a dancer, she said.</p><p>“I want to get ripped and wreak havoc,” she said. “I’d like to do something that requires some rigor, where I’d have to really learn something new.”</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="AnchorLink" class="Figure-content"><figcaption class="Figure-caption"><p>“I just want you to know that I don’t take it for granted,” Carrie Coon said while accepting the Artistic Achievement Award at the Chicago International Film Festival. “It’s hard work, but it’s also a lot of luck.”</p></figcaption><span class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Manuel Martinez/WBEZ</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>As parents of two children, ages 5 and 8, Coon and Letts also have to consider what’s best for their family when evaluating projects. But whether it’s Coon traveling to Thailand to film “White Lotus,” or Letts starring in “Death of a Salesman” at the National Theatre later in 2027, some jobs are too good for the New York residents to pass up.</p><p>“He's going to be a tremendous Willy Loman,” Coon said of her husband. “But for him to go to London and do a play for six months, that's going to be really hard.”</p><p>The couple also aspires to revive Letts’ Pulitzer Prize-winning play, “August Osage County,” which premiered at Steppenwolf Theatre nearly 20 years ago. Coon, who hopes to portray Barbara Fordham, believes the work is especially relevant today.</p><p>“Tracy’s work is always so prescient,” she said. “I think people will be stunned by the resonance in the way he's talking about this country in that play.”</p><p>These days, Coon’s political pursuits are not limited to the stage or screen. She has ramped up her activism, which includes campaigning for Caitlin Conley, the Democrat currently running against incumbent Rep. Mike Lawler in New York’s 17th district. She also has spoken out against President Trump’s deportation campaign. (She ended her speech at Music Box Theatre by yelling, “F— ICE!”)</p><p>She said her children have inspired her advocacy.</p><p>“I do feel it's incumbent upon me to be an example for them about what it means to be a good citizen and a good steward of your community,” she said.</p>

entries.title: Neighbors count down last breakfasts before ‘iconic’ Southport Grocery closes for Dollop Finer Diner
entries.summary: <p>Judy Sutton Taylor has been bringing her twin daughters to Southport Grocery and Cafe since they were born in 2003, the same year the iconic Lake View breakfast spot opened.</p><p>After hearing that Southport will close on Dec. 31, she and her friend Patti Morrow decided to grab the most important meal of the day on the patio. “I've been here countless times and just wanted to get in as many opportunities as we can to come before it closes,” Sutton Taylor said.</p><p>The closure of the beloved Lake View staple will make way for Dollop Finer Diner, an outpost of Chicago-based Dollop Coffee Co., which has multiple neighborhood cafes across the city. The new concept will feature specialty coffee and “elevated” breakfast and lunch items, said Southport owner and chef Lisa Santos. As with the 2026 closures of other upscale diners with decades of history, like <a class="Link" href="https://www.wbez.org/food-drink/2026/08/12/wishbone-restaurant-chicago-closing-west-loop" target="_blank" ><u>Wishbone in the West Loop</u></a>, neighbors and regulars like Sutton Taylor have lamented the loss of a family-friendly community gathering place that has been a generational staple.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="AnchorLink" id="image-480000" name="image-480000"></a> <picture Maybe a book, but not a cookbook?”</p><p>Santos said her decision to close is “twofold.” First, she’d always kept the inevitability of exiting in the back of her head, especially as a small business owner.</p><p>Nearly four years ago, Santos met with two leaders of Dollop Coffee Co.: Keith Kreuser, director of food and beverage, and Dan Weiss, the founder and CEO. Both teams were looking for ways to stay afloat, especially after COVID-19 changed the restaurant landscape in Chicago.</p><p>“Post-pandemic, we had closed our bake shop down at 1000 N. Damen Ave. and shoehorned … those operations into our Montrose location,” Kreuser said. entries.title: 10 ways to celebrate Día de Muertos in Chicago in 2026
entries.summary: <p>Halloween is this weekend. But after all of the spooky storytelling, costume contests and trick-or-treating, Día de Muertos, or Day of the Dead in English, happens each year on Nov. 1 and 2.</p><p>The holiday, with roots in indigenous Mesoamerican and Spanish Catholic traditions, has been celebrated in Mexico and Central Latin American countries for centuries. Most people associate it with the sugar skulls, marigolds and family photos that are placed on ofrendas — which, in English, are altars— inside people’s homes.</p><p>Families believe that the veil that exists between the natural world and the spiritual world thins out between Oct. 31 and Nov. 2, making way for our ancestors to come back to visit us for a few nights. In addition to the flowers and photos, people might leave out their deceased loved ones’ favorite foods, bottles of liquor or personal items.</p><p>The tradition has expanded beyond Latin America and into U.S. cities like Chicago, where some neighborhoods go all out for the celebration. Here are a few special ways to celebrate the holiday in Chicago.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="AnchorLink" W. 19th St. in Pilsen, this iconic museum does not charge an admission fee. Día de Muertos is a huge thing every year at the NMMA, and this year’s exhibition is titled <a class="Link" href="https://nationalmuseumofmexicanart.org/events/where-memory-lives" target="_blank" ><u>“Where Memory Lives: 40 Years of Día de Muertos.”</u></a> The 40th annual installation features artwork centered around themes of mortality, grief and loss, but it’s also a celebration of life.</p><p>The museum always dedicates the showcase to the deceased, and this year’s collection was curated by Dolores Mercado, Elisa Soto Sánchez and Cesáreo Moreno, and is dedicated to Dr. Gilberto Cárdenas, who died this summer. The museum’s website describes Cárdenas as a “dedicated scholar, pioneer of Chicano Studies, and a dear friend” of the museum. He “believed in the power of art to honor the histories and voices of Mexican, Chicana/o, and Latinx communities in the U.S.”</p><p>The following weekend, the museum will host its annual <a class="Link" href="https://nationalmuseumofmexicanart.org/events/dia-de-muertos-love-never-dies-ball-2" target="_blank" ><u>Love Never Dies Ball</u></a>. Guests will be dressed to impress in “creative cocktail” attire, colorful, elaborate dresses, dapper suits and, of course, plenty of face paint. The night includes performances from DJ Memo Duarte of <a class="Link" href="https://pachangachicago.com/" target="_blank" ><u>¡Pachanga! Chicago</u></a> and a cumbia group called Impakto Sonidero. Admission includes open galleries, cocktails, food and a silent auction. Tickets are $125 when purchased in advance, and $150 at the door.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a Sometimes, their deaths inspire a type of grief that’s just as strong as the way we mourn our fellow humans. Fortunately, pets of all kinds have their own special day in which their souls are welcomed back during Día de Muertos season each October. This year, the zoo received more than 300 submissions for Brookfield Zoo’s pet-themed ofrenda. The zoo worked with local florist Manuel Buenrostro, of Manny’s Flower Design in Northlake, to put the altar together. Halsted St. for a <a class="Link" href="https://larkchicago.com/events/latin-day-of-the-dead-bottomless-drag-brunch/" target="_blank" ><u>Day of the Dead drag show</u></a> on Sunday. With admission, you’ll get an entree — chilaquiles or fried chicken and pancakes — and bottomless alcoholic or nonalcoholic drinks for 90 minutes. Performers include <a class="Link" href="https://www.instagram.com/millusi0n/?hl=en" target="_blank" ><u>Milani</u></a>, La Más Mejor and <a class="Link" href="https://www.instagram.com/venuscarangi/?hl=en" target="_blank" ><u>Venus Carangi</u></a>. Grand Ave., where a <a class="Link" href="https://www.exploretock.com/thedawson/event/368059" target="_blank" ><u>$10 cover</u></a> grants you tequila and mezcal tastings in the upstairs lounge. Wells St., enjoy Day of the Dead-inspired cocktails made with mezcal, cempasúchil, mole and more. entries.title: Bears predictions: Week 8 at Seahawks
entries.summary: <p>The Sun-Times' experts make their picks for the “Monday Night Football” clash against the defending Super Bowl champion Seahawks:</p><h3><b>Patrick Finley</b></h3><p><b>Seahawks, 20-17: </b>The last time the Bears played a regular season game in Seattle, three inches of snow shut down the city and Nick Foles led the Bears to a win. <b>Season</b>: 3-4.</p><h3><b>Jason Lieser</b></h3><p><b>Seahawks, 24-20:</b> The defending champs, playing a prime-time game in one of the loudest stadiums in the NFL, look like they’re back on track after dominating the Chiefs. <b>Season:</b> 4-3.</p><h3><b>Scoop Jackson</b></h3><p><b>Bears, 32-30: </b>So far this season the defending champs have lost one game they weren’t supposed to lose (Washington) — and after last week’s punking of the Chiefs, they may only lose one more that’s predicted for them to win. This one. <b>Season</b>: 3-4.</p><h3><b>Steve Greenberg</b></h3><p><b>Seahawks, 24-19:</b> Say hello to the Bears' toughest test of the season, tangling with the NFL's top-ranked defense. The Emerald City wrecking crew held the previously unbeaten Chiefs to three points last time out. <b>Season</b>: 5-2.</p><h3><b>Jeff Agrest</b></h3><p><b>Seahawks, 24-14: </b>Caleb Williams has passer ratings of over 110 in three of his four games. The one outlier is a 56.2 mark, which came against the Vikings’ now-second-ranked defense. Facing the Seahawks’ top-ranked defense in the toughest venue for opponents will lead to a similar fate. <b>Season</b>: 3-4.</p>

Owings and Merrill has released renderings of a plan that would put the Bears in a new domed stadium at the Rate Field site in Bridgeport — and potentially help bolster a plan for the White Sox to move to the South Loop. href="https://newsletters.suntimes.com/t/t-l-yddrkjll-l-tu/" target="_blank" >Pat Nabong</a> and <a class="Link" href="https://newsletters.suntimes.com/t/t-l-yddrkjll-l-il/" target="_blank" >Mary Norkol</a></h5><p>Met with cheers, T-shirts and voter guides, hundreds of Chicago high school students flooded the Loop early voting supersite Wednesday as part of a push for young voter participation.</p><p>Chicago Votes, a political organization with a focus on young people, sponsored the Parade to the Polls, busing students from school to the Loop site so they could cast their ballots in the upcoming general election, many of them for the first time. Each time a rookie voter cast their ballot, an election official rang a bell to congratulate them.</p><p>"I was a little nervous, but ... I understood what I was potentially going to be voting for and overall I’m just really happy that I got to vote," said Pritzker College Prep student Elijah Candelaria.</p><p><a class="Link" href="https://newsletters.suntimes.com/t/t-l-yddrkjll-l-ir/" target="_blank" ><b>READ MORE</b></a></p><hr><p></p><h4>YOUR DAILY QUESTION ☕️</h4><p><b>What's your defining memory of Halloween as a kid growing up in the Chicago area? 🎃</b></p><p><a class="Link" href="mailto:newsletters@suntimes.com" target="_blank" ><i>Reply to this question via email</i></a><i> (please include your first and last name). We may run your answer in a future newsletter or story.</i></p><p>On Thursday, we asked you: <a class="Link" href="https://newsletters.suntimes.com/t/t-l-yddrkjll-l-ij/" target="_blank" >What’s the best Chicago-set TV show of all time?</a></p><p>Here’s some of what you said, edited for length and clarity:</p><p>"I loved 'Early Edition' with Kyle Chandler who received a special Sun-Times issue each day — 'special' because it arrived a day early, allowing him to change events before they would happen. ... All sorts of plots/genres could be accommodated, but the main character was a relatable 'everyman' who strived to always do the right thing." — <i>Paul Lockwood</i></p><p>"'The Bob Newhart Show' was the absolute best TV show set in Chicago. With the brilliance of Bob Newhart and Suzanne Pleshette it has lasted through the years. I still watch reruns and can't stop laughing. The shots of Chicago remind me of my younger years. Fantastic!" — <i>Joan Roe</i></p><p>"'The Bear!' Chicago was not just the setting but one of the main characters in this show." — <i>Janet Volk</i></p><p>"'Bozo's Circus' — it has everything: comedy, suspense of the bucket game, live circus acts and magicians!" — <i>Gene Daly</i></p><hr><p>Thanks for reading the Sun-Times Morning Edition! Got a story you think we missed? <a class="Link" href="mailto:newsletters@suntimes.com" target="_blank" >Email us here.</a></p><hr><p><b>Written and curated by</b>: Matt Moore<br><b>Editor</b>: Michael Lansu<br><b>Copy edited by</b>: Satchel Price</p>

entries.title: Bears trading for Titans DT Jeffery Simmons
entries.summary: <p>The <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears" target="_blank" >Bears</a> have made a massive swing to improve their defense, agreeing to trade for four-time Titans Pro Bowl defensive tackle Jeffery Simmons on Thursday.</p><p>The Bears will give up two first-round picks and a fourth-rounder, per NFL Network, and get Simmons and a 2028 fifth-round pick back. That's the biggest package the Bears have sent out since former GM Ryan Pace traded for Khalil Mack in 2018.</p><p>Pushing their chips in for Simmons is a sign the Bears believe they have a chance to win the Super Bowl. They're 5-2 entering Monday night's game against the defending Super Bowl champion Seahawks despite having to start three different quarterbacks this year.</p><p>Simmons is one of the best defensive tackles on the planet. The Titans signed him to a three-year, $105.8 million extension before the season began. The Titans have already paid $20 million of his signing bonus. He's has a $22.5 million cap hit next year, a $30.9 million cap hit in 2028 and a $29.1 million hit in 2029.</p><p>The Bears faced Simmons in a joint practice during training camp. Coach Ben Johnson called Simmons a "bell cow" of "an attacking front." He has 46 1/2 sacks in eight seasons and is considered a premier run-stopper.</p><p>The Bears entered the season with concerns about their edge rushers — something that grew even louder after Dayo Odeyinbo was hurt and Montez Sweat served a two-game drug suspension. Simmons will be able to help from the inside — he's the sixth-highest-rated pass rusher among defensive tackles, per Pro Football Focus.</p><p>Simmons figures to slot next to Grady Jarrett in the Bears' starting lineup. The team traded Gervon Dexter to the Falcons before the start of the season and has since been using a rotation that includes Dexter, Kentavius Street, Neville Gallimore and Jordan van den Berg.</p><p>Simmons, who turned 29 in July, was the 19th pick of the 2019 draft out of Mississippi State.<br></p>

entries.title: DoorDash offers $17 billion for Instacart in what would be a big consolidation for grocery delivery
entries.summary: <p>DoorDash is offering $17 billion to buy Instacart to supercharge its grocery delivery business in what would be a big consolidation in grocery delivery.</p><p>DoorDash said the Instacart brand name and app will remain, and Instacart shoppers would be able to continue fulfilling orders as before. Grocers can also choose to work with Instacart or DoorDash. Instacart customers will now have access to 50,000 additional stores covered by DoorDash, the company said.</p><p>Instacart, founded in 2012, specializes in grocery and convenience store delivery in the U.S. and Canada. Its 600,000 “shoppers” — who are independent contractors — completed 338 million orders last year, according to company filings. Instacart has a market value of $14 billion.</p><p>DoorDash, founded in San Francisco in 2013, began as a restaurant delivery business but has expanded to pet food and electronics. Operating in 40 countries, it completed more than 3 billion orders last year using a network of 9 million independent delivery workers. It has a market value of $73 billion.</p><p>DoorDash began delivering groceries in 2020, amid a surge in pandemic-era demand. Grocers were initially cautious. Kroger partnered with the San Francisco company in 2022 but initially allowed the company to deliver only flowers, sushi and prepared meals from a limited number of stores.</p><p>The partnership with one of the nation’s largest grocery chains expanded last fall, and DoorDash now lists the full inventory of all 2,700 U.S. Kroger stores in its online marketplace. DoorDash scored another coup last month when it added delivery from Costco.</p><p>DoorDash co-founder and CEO Tony Xu said the acquisition will combine Instacart’s expertise in grocery with DoorDash’s expertise in logistics and delivery.</p><p>“Grocery is one of the hardest things to get right online. Someone has to pick a ripe avocado, find a substitute you’d choose yourself, and get the ice cream to you before it melts,” Xu said in a statement. “Together, we could give stores of every size more of those tools and unlock the potential of grocery delivery.”</p><p>DoorDash’s aggressive market-share gains by have hurt Instacart. Five years ago, Instacart commanded 26% of spending on U.S. delivery platforms; that share has fallen to 18%, according to market research company Consumer Edge. DoorDash’s share grew from 44% to 59% in that same period. Uber Eats’ share held steady at just under 20%.</p><p>It’s not yet clear what the deal will mean for some partnerships. Instacart offers delivery from Walmart, for example, but DoorDash stopped providing Walmart delivery in 2022.</p>

entries.title: Four-year lineman Christian Malachuk, Nazareth preparing for long road trip, title run
entries.summary: <p>Christian Malachuk has his priorities in order as he prepares for Nazareth’s near three-hour bus ride to Dunlap on Saturday.</p><p>“Definitely prioritizing sleep this week, especially playing Saturday at 1:30 p.m., bus ride is going to be a lot longer than we’re used to,” Malachuk said. “Got to keep the body fresh and the mind fresh.”</p><p>Malachuk speaks from experience, which makes sense. A four-year lineman, this will be the Nazareth senior’s 52nd time putting on a varsity uniform, all but the first five games freshman year as a starter.</p><p>The CCL Lineman of the Year as a junior, Malachuk’s experience is invaluable for a young Nazareth line that starts two juniors and a sophomore around him and Missouri commit Luke Injaychock.</p><p>“His stats and his past performance speak for themselves,” Nazareth coach Tim Racki said. “It’s hard to be a four-year starter on the line. He’s not only managed it, but excelled at it. Extremely high football IQ, which is a blessing with blocking schemes having younger guys.”</p><p>“The sixth man” on Nazareth’s line the first five weeks of his freshman year, Malachuk got his first start at left guard the sixth game when the team’s right tackle was hurt.</p><p>Malachuk quickly learned what it would take to compete on the line in the CCL.</p><p>“Freshman year I was 225 pounds, I knew going into sophomore year I had to put on a lot of muscle,” said Malachuk, now 6-foot and 290 pounds. “Some of the kids we play in this league are freaks. I mean, it’s unreal. I had to develop my body, develop my mind.”</p><p>He’s been everywhere on the line since.</p><p>Malachuk started at left guard as a freshman, right tackle his sophomore year and left tackle as a junior. This year, he was moved to center and is also playing some defense.</p><p>“It helps tremendously putting him at center,” Racki said. “He’s able to communicate all of the checks and blocking schemes, makes it easier on the coaching staff.</p><p>“He can play any spot on the line with his athleticism. He is extremely athletic for his size with his footwork and technique. He’s always been a solid technician – that’s how he broke into the lineup as a freshman. He’s got some toughness and tenacity and competitiveness and he thrives in his leadership position.”</p><p>Malachuk is the second of three brothers to come through the Nazareth program. His younger brother Gavin is a junior playing outside linebacker.</p><p>Older brother Logan, a 5-11, 190-pound quarterback, broke an IHSA record for career passing yards while leading Nazareth to three straight state titles in 2022-24.</p><p>What about that size disparity between brothers?</p><p>“Our mom is 5 feet tall. It happens. We are doing our best to make it with what we’ve got,” Christian Malachuk said with a laugh. “I’m really grateful to use my talents.”</p><p>Malachuk would love nothing more than to add one more state title to the family legacy.</p><p>He was a freshman on the 2023 team that made history by winning a Class 5A state championship after going 4-5 during the regular season. This Nazareth group hopes history repeats itself in Class 6A.</p><p>“Having that 4-5 record makes us seem like the underdogs and we play that much better,” Malachuk said. “I definitely remember looking up to the senior leaders, especially my older brother. That junior and senior class was special to me, taught me everything I know. The culture coach builds is really special. We are so connected and strong as a team. No matter who we play, we’ll give it our all.”</p><p><a class="Link" href="https://www.shawlocal.com/friday-night-drive/" target="_blank" >Read more high school football coverage at Friday Night Drive.</a></p>

entries.title: Bears-Seahawks game Monday night will air in Chicago on ESPN, The U — not ABC 7
entries.summary: <p>The Bears' game Monday night against the Seahawks will be available over the air in Chicago, but in an unusual place. </p><p>Though ESPN is broadcasting the game on cable, fellow Disney channel ABC 7 won't carry it because of an episode of "Dancing With the Stars." Instead, The U (WCIU-Channel 26) will be the game's over-the-air home. The decision not to air the game on ABC's local affiliate was made by the network.</p><p>The NFL has a long-standing policy requiring games on cable or a streaming service to be available over the air in the teams’ local markets. The last time the Bears appeared on The U was Nov. 16, 2020, a Monday, against the Vikings.</p><p>The Bears aren't the first Chicago team to get bumped from ABC 7 to The U. On Sept. 17, 2019, the Cubs' game against the Reds moved because of the season finale of "Bachelor in Paradise." At the time, ABC 7 aired a package of Cubs games along with NBC Sports Chicago and WGN 9.</p><p>The U will carry an ABC 7-produced pregame show, "Monday Night Monsters," at 6:30 p.m. hosted by Ryan Chiaverini and Dionne Miller. ESPN's broadcast will begin at 7, with Joe Buck and Troy Aikman calling the game at 7:15.</p><p>ESPN2 will air the ManningCast, "Monday Night Football with Peyton & Eli," an alternative broadcast starring the former NFL quarterbacks. The show will announce its guests Monday.</p><p>The Bears' run of three consecutive standalone games ends Nov. 8 at home against the Buccaneers on NBC's "Sunday Night Football." That game undoubtedly will air on NBC 5 in Chicago.</p>

entries.title: Newborn dies after teen gives birth at Far South Side school
entries.summary: <p>Police are investigating following the death of a newborn whose teen mother gave gave birth at a Far South Side school Wednesday afternoon in the Riverdale neighborhood.</p><p>The 15-year-old girl gave birth around 3 p.m. Wednesday at Aldridge Elementary School, 630 E. 131st St., where the baby was pronounced dead, according to Chicago police and the Cook County medical examiner's office. </p><p>The teen was taken to Comer Children's Hospital where she was in good condition, police said. </p><p>Chicago Public Schools have not yet responded to a request for comment. </p><p>Area 2 detectives are investigating. </p>
