entries.title: Oficiales dicen que agente del FBI fuera de servicio mató a hombre que disparaba contra una multitud en Pilsen
entries.summary: <p>Un agente del FBI que estaba fuera de servicio disparó y mató a un hombre que vio disparar contra una multitud en Pilsen el lunes por la noche, dijo la agencia en un comunicado.</p><p>El agente conducía hacia su casa del trabajo en un vehículo del FBI alrededor de las 5:30 p.m. cuando vio al hombre “disparando un arma contra un grupo de personas inocentes” cerca de la calle 18th y Union Avenue, según el FBI. Se escucharon al menos dos disparos antes de que el agente interviniera “para detener la amenaza en curso”, dijo el FBI.</p><p>Cuando los policías de Chicago acudieron tras una llamada por un agente en peligro alrededor de la hora del tiroteo, encontraron al agente de 41 años apuntando al agresor después de haberlo herido, según un informe de la Policía de Chicago. En el informe se indicó que se encontró una pistola debajo de una bicicleta.</p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-center><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-1c0000" name="module-1c0000"></a> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody"><h3>La Voz Chicago WhatsApp</h3>Encuentra más noticias en nuestro canal de WhatsApp. <a class="Link" href="https://www.whatsapp.com/channel/0029Vb0XT1XCHDylm3rCs40P" target="_blank" ><b>Síguenos.</b></a></div> </div><p>El agresor, identificado como Oscar Isaya Corrales, de 27 años de edad, había sufrido heridas por bala en ambas piernas, en el pecho y en el flanco derecho, según el informe policial y la Oficina del Forense del Condado de Cook.</p><p>Isaya Corrales fue posteriormente declarado muerto en el Hospital Stroger, menos de una hora después de haber sido baleado, dijeron las autoridades. Su muerte fue calificada como homicidio, según la oficina del forense.</p><p>El FBI dijo que el agente no resultó herido. Un agente con el mismo nombre que figura en el informe policial se incorporó al FBI en marzo de 2017 y también había trabajado en Seattle, según documentos de la corte federal.</p><p>“El FBI se toma en serio todos los incidentes de disparos que involucran a nuestros agentes o a miembros de nuestros equipos”, dijo la agencia en un comunicado. “Conforme a la política del FBI, el incidente de disparos está siendo revisado por la División de Inspección del FBI”.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item"> <bsp-carousel class="Carousel Enhancement" entries.title: So RFK Jr's dismissing Arab, Muslim contributions to society? If he’s in the Loop, he can just look around.
entries.summary: <p>People ask me directions. All the time. I'm not sure why. Maybe because I have a friendly face, maybe because I’m the most unmenacing man ever: 5'9”, almost, gray and balding, wearing glasses and an REI fleece that can't go out of style because it never was in.</p><p>I'm glad they do. Because I like giving directions. Makes me feel useful. My favorite moment came when standing at the corner of Michigan and Chestnut. A couple approached, clutching a guidebook, asking, in heavily French-accented English, if I would be so kind as to direct them to zee Hancock Building. I slowly lifted my finger to point at the brownish black, criss-crossed tower looming directly in front of us, smiled and said, <i>"Voila.</i>"</p><p>Which, forgive me, I feel obligated to do now that the Trump administration is turning up their racism to 11 in the final sprint to Tuesday's election. Particularly the Secretary of Health and Human Services, Robert F. Kennedy Jr., who said:</p><p>"There's 500 million Arabs in the world. And yet they don't produce science. They don't win the Nobel Prize. They don't win the Fields Prize. They don't win the Wolf Prize. They don't produce literature."</p><p>He's wrong in all particulars, as usual. I count three Muslims who've won the Fields Medal — not "prize," doofus — the top award in mathematics. Several have won a Wolf Prize.</p><p>I understand I'm shifting populations here — Arabs and Muslims overlap, but are not the same group. "Arab" is an ethnic identity, which RFK Jr. is using as code for "Muslim," a religious designation. There are Arab Christians and, while they don't get much press, Arab Jews. (H.L. Mencken, in his epic "The American Language," lists "arab" as a slur for Jews.)</p><p>Before we get completely off track, pause to savor the head-spinning hypocrisy of RFK Jr. invoking the Fields Medal and the Wolf Prize, for excellence in science. In the mouth of a man who disgraced himself through vigorous anti-science, whose unwavering devotion to nutty folk belief has literally killed children.</p><p>It's such an uncharacteristic pivot, this sudden passion for achievement. You'll never hear Trump lecture his torch-wielding nationalist buddies, "You know, you're kinda hard on Jews, considering they've won Nobel Prizes up the wazoo."</p><p>Consistency isn't their strong suit.</p><p>If I addressed the fabrications (to use the word favored by the New York Times) and lies (shorter, more to the point, but a buzz kill, apparently, for those committed to not grasping what is going on) it's all I'd ever do. But this particular bigotry is being so strongly directed at surging Muslim politicians like Michigan U.S. Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed (whose position on Israel will matter to me once we secure democracy at home) that I have to address it, especially since I know many readers share RFK Jr.'s mistaken notions.</p><p>So you blunder up to me downtown, drawn by my open, honest, inviting mug, and ask, "But they really haven't made many contributions since Arabic numbers, right?"</p><p>And I smile, making eye contract, while slowly lifting both arms, one finger pointing at the former Hancock Building (now, <i>shiver,</i><i> </i>875 N. Michigan) the other at the Willis Tower, and say: "Fazlur Rahman Khan, 'the Einstein of structural engineering,' did the design work on both buildings, partnering with architect Bruce Graham at Skidmore, Owings & Merrill.</p><p>Chicagoans hurry past every day, and don't know the story. They don't know that Khan never even <i>saw </i>a skyscraper until he was 21; no building in the city, Dhaka, Bangladesh, where he grew up was more than three stories. He probably couldn't get into the United States today — too brown, too Muslim — but came to the University of Illinois in 1952, earning two masters degrees in three years, one in structural engineering, another in theoretical and applied mechanics.</p><p>At the time, the height of skyscrapers was limited by the weight of steel beams — the higher the building, the heavier the steel, the more wind force working against it. Inspired by the hollow bamboo common in his homeland, Khan devised the tubular system that allowed the Sears Tower to rise to 110 stories. He also convinced Skidmore to buy an expensive mainframe computer to try this new computer-aided design, which he felt had a future.</p><p>Maybe the next time RFK Jr. is listing awards he imagines "arabs" don't win, he can mention the Fazlur Khan Lifetime Achievement Medal, awarded by the Council on Tall Buildings and Urban Habitat to individuals who have “demonstrated excellence in technical design and/or research that has made a significant contribution to a discipline for the design of tall buildings and the built urban environment." Khan never won, the award being created in his honor in 2004, 22 years after his death at age 52 in 1982.</p>

entries.title: Alleged burglars spark police chase that ends with crash, arrests on Eisenhower in west suburbs
entries.summary: <p>Several suspected burglars who were allegedly driving stolen vehicles were arrested early Thursday after a police pursuit ended in a crash on the Eisenhower Expressway in the western suburbs, Addison police said. </p><p>Around 4:35 a.m., detectives were watching several gaming locations due to recent burglary activity when they noticed a Dodge Durango with no license plates and a BMW pull into the parking lot of Maria’s Gaming Cafe at 40 East Lake, Addison police said. </p><p>The occupants of the vehicles forced their way into the cafe — which had been prone to prior burglaries — and took items from inside before fleeing, officials said. </p><p>Spike strips were deployed on the BMW to disable it and the occupants moved into the Durango which then fled onto the Eisenhower, police said.</p><p>After a pursuit involving several agencies, the Durango was halted using "stop mitigation devices" near I-290 and 25th Avenue near Bellwood and, after a short foot chase, several suspects were taken into custody, police said. </p><p>Several guns and burglary proceeds have been recovered and both vehicles were reported stolen, authorities said. </p><p>Illinois State Police troopers assisted in the crash, according to a spokesperson. Three lanes were shut down on I-290 eastbound, west of 25th Ave., and reopened at approximately 6:05 a.m. The investigation was ongoing.<br></p>

entries.title: Painter Mary Cassatt created a masterpiece for the 1893 World’s Fair in Chicago. Then, it disappeared.
entries.summary: <p>The Art Institute of Chicago’s <a class="Link" href="https://www.wbez.org/arts/2026/09/08/mary-cassatt-after-impressionism-art-institute-chicago-paintings-impressionist-mural-worlds-fair-1893" target="_blank" ><u>fall blockbuster shows the work</u></a> of impressionist painter Mary Cassatt. And at the exhibit’s heart is an art mystery.</p><p>The show tells the story of the giant, three-panel mural that Cassatt created for the 1893 World’s Fair in Chicago. However, the piece itself is missing. After the fair ended, it went into storage and was never seen again.</p><p>“The last known location is 1912 here in Chicago, and then the paper trail ends,” said curator Annelise Madsen. “One of the objectives of the exhibition is to piece together that story and try to bring it back to life for visitors. It’s such an important part of Chicago history.”</p><div class="Enhancement FormEnhancement" data-align-center> <div id="Form-newsletter-wrapper" class="Form-newsletter-wrapper" data-module class="Figure-content"><figcaption class="Figure-caption"><p>Mary Cassatt’s mural “Modern Woman” hangs inside the Woman’s Building in the 1893 World’s Columbian Exposition, as pictured in Hubert Howe Bancroft’s “The Book of the Fair” (Bancroft, 1893), 3:269.<br></p></figcaption></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>The murals were an enormous physical undertaking and represented a rare opportunity for women artists of the day. Cassatt’s work stretched 60 feet long and 14 feet high. Three scenes show well-dressed women chasing after a metaphor for fame, playing music and tending to an orchard. That scene in the middle signifies women plucking the fruits of knowledge and science.</p><p>Together, Cassatt’s massive work showed, “the possibilities today of women becoming educated, becoming artists, and actually seeking fame, just as she, Mary Cassatt, herself had sought,” said Corn.</p><p>After the fair, the Woman’s Building, like most others, was destroyed. Cassatt’s mural and other artwork were put in storage. Madsen said the last known location was in the Palmer family’s Gold Coast mansion, which was located on Lake Shore Drive and was once the largest private residence in the city before it was demolished in 1950.</p><p>Around 1912, the then-director of the Art Institute wrote a letter to inquire about unrolling the mural to see if it could be installed temporarily at the museum.</p><p>“That paper trail is in the Art Institute's archives, and it ends with the director wondering about whether it could come out again, and it just didn't happen,” Madsen said.</p><p>There’s speculation the piece was damaged by water or perhaps burned in a fire. But could Cassatt’s mural still be out there? Corn says: Not likely.</p><p>“So many women have looked for it. And they seem to have done an awful lot of work to pretty much determine that it is gone,” Corn said. “So I don't think there's a chance that it would show.”</p><p>Still, the mural did help to solidify Cassatt’s reputation in the States. And, it paved the way for women artists</p><p>“If you're going to look for women doing large paintings, you're probably going to start your story in 1893,” Corn said. “And then follow it thereafter as other women stepped up and took on more larger paintings and larger commissions.”</p><p><i>Courtney Kueppers is an arts and culture reporter at WBEZ. </i></p>

entries.title: Rise and pine: The Score's 'Haugh & Payton' showing inexperience in new roles
entries.summary: <p>A morning radio show is supposed to wake up its listeners, activate their brains and entertain them.</p><p>Two months into its existence, The Score’s “Haugh & Payton” show is 0-for-3.</p><p>Those who tune in have been subjected to two co-hosts who are learning on the job, which isn’t befitting of a show in a sports-crazed town that’s the third-largest market in the country.</p><p>How can you tell? Allow me to explain.</p><p>Last week, a man called the show from prison to talk about the Bears’ victory against the Falcons. Yes, from PRISON. It was one of the few times I perked up listening to the show. He questioned coach Ben Johnson’s decision to pull the defensive starters early, which helped the Falcons get back in the game.</p><p>David Haugh complimented the question — he’s a caller’s best friend — and asked the man where he was calling from. To make sure he was part of the conversation, Jarrett Payton interjected with, “Yeah.” The man said he was in Waupun prison in Wisconsin.</p><p>“I actually had a marijuana case in Illinois and ended up here for a gun violation,” he said. “Needless to say, I love the Bears. My uncle’s got season tickets. I watch the game every Sunday. Just a big NFL fan.”</p><p>Haugh and Payton thanked him for calling, gave him their answers and moved on. I thought, “Wow, they should’ve done a lot more than that.”</p><p>This wasn’t Bill from Berwyn calling. It was a prisoner of the state. Back in sports radio’s heyday, that would’ve been manna from heaven. Can you imagine the conversation Terry Boers and Dan Bernstein would’ve had with him?</p><p>That’s the kind of situation where Haugh, a longtime newspaper man, and Payton, a longtime TV man, show their inexperience in radio. Add in the fact that Haugh is driving the show (radio term) full-time for the first time, and there’s a lot of learning going on for everyone to hear.</p><p>Let’s start with Haugh, the incumbent co-host. People have told me that I write the way I talk. Having read and listened to Haugh, there might be something to that, because he used to write long and now he talks long. (I know I’ve written that before, but it’s fun to do.)</p><p>He’s in a tough spot. Mike Mulligan was the show driver before The Score fired him in August. Now Haugh is running things and perhaps trying to compensate — intentionally or subconsciously — while Payton acclimates to talking for 4½ hours instead of 30 minutes.</p><p>Haugh spews a lot of thoughts and information, but he’s just talking. It’s easy to zone out listening to him. For all the video streams of radio broadcasts, it’s still an audio medium first. Talking on the air is a learned skill, and there’s a performative element to it that he lacks.</p><p>Payton has it. He has a personality and a way of talking that can grab your attention. He just needs more things to say that aren’t about University of Miami football. He either is leaning on executive producer Dustin Rhoades to fill in the gaps or Rhoades darn well knows he needs to fill in the gaps because the show might as well be called “Haugh, Payton & Rhoades.”</p><p>The Score ran a promo that declared, “Jarrett Payton is bringing it on the ‘Haugh and Payton’ show.” That was followed by Payton saying, “My biggest surprise was Caleb Williams, where the ball was coming out of his hand, and I’m going, ‘Holy cow, this dude can spin it.’ He is special. I didn’t know he was gonna be that efficient.”</p><p>If that’s bringing it, imagine if he likes someone.</p><p>But Payton has shown he can mix it up. In another rare moment that caught my attention, Haugh and Payton were interviewing Bulls coach Tiago Splitter when Splitter said he didn’t like to hear his voice. Haugh asked why that was.</p><p>“I guess nobody likes to hear their own voice,” Splitter said.</p><p>To which Payton said, “Coach, David does.”</p><p>Haugh laughed and took it in good fun, as he should’ve. With two other shows on The Score and two on Chicago Sports Network, Haugh should get some ribbing. Guys busting other guys’ you-know-what is part of sports radio. More of that, please.</p><p>But don’t hold your breath. Neither seems willing to deliver a strong, unique opinion. Haugh doesn’t take enough stands, and Payton spews too many clichés. Sometimes he sounds like an athlete after a game, which, in fact, he was. Did you know he played at Miami?</p><p>“It’s about taking advantage of your situation and focus on what you need to get better at,” Payton said of the Bears, sending my pupils higher in my head.</p><p>Boers used to open every “Boers & Bernstein” show saying, “We’re going to do the best we can to keep you informed, entertained, perhaps have a laugh or two along the way.” By that criterion, “Haugh & Payton” are 1-for-3. All those words provide some information of value.</p><p>They’re going to have to learn on the job much faster to make the show better.</p>
entries.author: Jeff Agrest

entries.title: Bridgeport Bears? Chicago firm releases plans for glitzy new domed stadium at Sox park site
entries.summary: <p>A Chicago architectural firm on Wednesday released renderings of a plan that would put the Bears in a new domed stadium at the Rate Field site — and potentially help bolster a plan for the Chicago White Sox to move to the South Loop.</p><p>Skidmore, Owings and Merrill posted the renderings to their Instagram page Wednesday, saying the plan would create a new home for the Bears with a mixed-use district that would bring together housing, entertainment, hospitality, parks and public recreation. The firm noted the transportation infrastructure already is in place at the site in Armour Square, adjacent to the Bridgeport neighborhood, with access to the CTA, Metra and Dan Ryan Expressway.</p> <p>Renderings of the plan being distributed to stakeholders say the stadium and campus are "presented by Sterling Bay." But Sterling Bay CEO Andy Gloor in a text message told the Chicago Sun-Times the plan is a Skidmore "work product" and said Sterling Bay is "not driving this deal although we love the idea of keeping the Bears in Chicago."</p><p>Even so, a spokesperson from Sterling Bay called the plan "a real viable solution to keeping the Bears in Chicago."</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div large amount of publicly owned land surrounding the site that could transform the stadium into a district with more affordable and market-rate housing, civic amenities and new and improved pedestrian bridges to bring lasting vitality to the surrounding neighborhoods,” the architectural firm said.</p><p>Sources said the plan would include moving Wentworth Gardens, a nearby CHA housing development, which would certainly meet some resistance.</p><p>But a Bears stadium at the site, which is owned by the Illinois Sports Facilities Authority, could mean the team could avoid paying property taxes, a major selling point. There’s also the built-in infrastructure, with the potential for federal transportation funds as well.</p><p>All of the chatter comes as Canal Edge LLC — a company owned by White Sox minority owner Justin Ishbia — released plans in September for a mixed-use development called the Railyards, which would <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/white-sox/2026/09/05/new-sox-park-future-owner-announces-proposal-for-riverside-stadium-at-the-railyards" >move the Chicago White Sox </a>to the South Loop. The baseball stadium would sit alongside the Chicago River on a site stretching from Roosevelt Road on the north to 18th Street on the south, bordered by the river on the east and Canal Street to the west.</p><p>But putting the stadium at that riverfront location requires moving an Amtrak maintenance yard, and the move came hand-in-hand with <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/white-sox/2025/06/06/justin-ishbia-white-sox-jerry-reinsdorf-ownership-winnetka" target="_blank" ><u>Ishbia</u></a>’s companies helping to finance moving the Amtrak facility to Bridgeport.</p><p>That plan has met some major community resistance because Amtrak initially had received more than $600 million and a “<a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/white-sox/what-to-know-chicago-white-sox-stadium-proposal-justin-ishbia" target="_blank" ><u>categorical exclusion</u></a>” from the federal government for the project, which allowed it to move forward without a full environmental assessment or an environmental impact statement “unless there are extraordinary circumstances.”</p><p>However, the Federal Railroad Administration this week said that the proposed Amtrak maintenance facility in Bridgeport would undergo a federal environmental review after that community pushback.</p><p>Mayor Brandon Johnson's office on Wednesday offered few details, saying in a statement to the Sun-Times that “the Mayor knows that Chicago is and should remain the home of the Bears and will continue to work with stakeholders across the region to do so.”</p><p>Eleventh Ward Ald. Nicole Lee said she is intrigued by the possibility of the Bears replacing the Sox at the site that now includes Rate Field, even though there are more far more questions than answers about the eleventh-hour plan. Lee and Cook County Commissioner John Daley have been embroiled in the battle with Amtrak and Ishbia to prevent the Sox from leaving Rate Field for the South Loop. That plan also entails the construction of the Amtrak maintenance site.</p><p>“I’m absolutely interested in conversations about what’s possible on this land — especially because the Sox haven’t necessarily talked to us about what it would take for them to stay,” Lee said Wednesday.</p><p>“The plans are — they’re real pretty pictures. entries.title: White Sox hiring Matt Roffe away from Brewers to fill open amateur scouting director role
entries.summary: <p>Powered by a top-flight player acquisition and development engine, the Milwaukee Brewers are World Series champions. The White Sox would love to emulate their Wisconsin neighbors’ ability to thrive despite a low major-league payroll, and are going about it in the most direct way possible.</p><p>Sources tell the Sun-Times that the Sox are expected to hire Matt Roffe to head up their draft operations. Roffe has spent the last five years with the Brewers, and was promoted to be their assistant director of domestic scouting last November. The hire has not been formally announced, and while general manager Chris Getz has previously said the Sox were hiring a “director of amateur acquisitions,” Roffe’s specific title has yet to be determined.</p><p>Either way, Roffe’s addition will fill a leadership role in the organization that has been vacant since amateur scouting director <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/white-sox/2026/09/12/white-sox-amateur-scouting-director-mike-shirley-resigns-chris-getz-garrett-crochet-colson-montgomery-grant-taylor-jacob-gonzalez-hagen-smith-caleb-bonemer" >Mike Shirley resigned in September,</a> amid what sources indicated was an internal investigation into his personal conduct. Two months prior to that, Shirley oversaw the White Sox selecting UCLA shortstop Roch Cholowsky with the first overall pick in the 2026 MLB Draft.</p><p>Before his departure, Shirley was the rare White Sox executive in baseball operations under Getz who had been retained from the Ken Williams/Rick Hahn era. Since taking over in August of 2023, Getz has hired three assistant general managers, directors for both their hitting and pitching departments, a director of acquisitions, a special assistant in charge of international scouting, and a director of player development; all of whom were brought in from outside the organization.</p><p>Multiple internal candidates from the Sox amateur scouting department were interviewed this month to fill Shirley’s role, according to sources. But pulling in Roffe from both a successful organization, and one defined by a regularly dominant farm system rather than financial muscle, fits a pattern established by Getz, and matches comments he made last month about the future of the department.</p><p>“We’re looking at a lot of different ways–we’ve been doing that for a while–not just a clear restructure, but a different way of doing business on that front,” Getz said in September. “If that means you’re going outside of the organization, so be it.”</p><p>As it turns out, the White Sox have gone outside of the organization in pursuit of an up-and-comer in the amateur scouting world. Roffe’s public profile is pretty under the radar, but it’s hard to quibble with where the Sox chose to shop.</p>

entries.title: Bears injury report: RB Kyle Monangai remains out
entries.summary:
The Bears' first injury report of the week doesn't bode well for Kyle Monangai's return Monday.

The running back was the only player that would have practiced Thursday had the Bears held one. Instead, they issued an estimated participation report, the first of Seahawks week. They'll hold a full practice Friday and Saturday.

Monangai suffered a turf toe injury against the Jets in Week 4 and hasn't played since.

Linebacker D'Marco Jackson, who had an interception in the end zone against the Patriots last week, would have been limited with an ankle injury and rookie cornerback Malik Muhammad would have been limited with a toe problem. Linebackers T.J. Edwards (hamstring) and Jack Sanborn (concussion) would have been full participants, laying out a path for them to play Monday night.

Also Thursday, the Bears cut defensive end Jamree Kromah and signed cornerback Josh Butler, who played for defensive backs coach Al Harris, to the practice squad.

entries.title: Moritz Seider knows why Artyom Levshunov looks more comfortable this Blackhawks season
entries.summary: <p>DETROIT — Experience is helpful for any NHL player, but it could be especially helpful for <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/blackhawks" target="_blank" >Blackhawks</a> defenseman Artyom Levshunov.</p><p>That's partly because, as has been discussed thoroughly over the past two-plus years, Levshunov was very raw when the Hawks drafted him — even compared to other first-round picks in his draft class.</p><p>He was physically mature, but he had relatively a long way to go in terms of mental maturity and understanding how to play hockey at the highest level. His rawness was evident during his chaotic 2025-26 rookie season, and his growth process has been equally <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/blackhawks/2026/10/08/blackhawks-artyom-levshunov-following-instincts-blues-anton-frondell" >evident</a> so far this season.</p><p>But that experience could be especially helpful also partly because Levshunov, who celebrated his 21st birthday Wednesday, plays so much better when relying on instincts instead of calculations. Over-thinking is his Achilles' heel. And experience reduces over-thinking.</p><p>Hawks coach Jeff Blashill has <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/blackhawks/2026/03/16/blackhawks-artyom-levshunov-defense-improved-moritz-seider-jeff-blashill" >compared</a> Levshunov to Red Wings stalwart Moritz Seider several times, referencing how it took Seider a while to reach his peak as arguably one of the top 10 defensemen in the league.</p><p>Seider said Thursday he hopes he still hasn't reached his peak yet, but he agreed he benefited greatly from the experience he accumulated during his first couple NHL seasons (2021-22 and 2022-23).</p><p>"It's almost like you're creating a toolbox, playing against all those players for numerous years," Seider said. "You know their tendencies. You know what certain lines have for playing styles, what certain power plays like to do. </p><p>"[Eventually], it happens automatically. You don't think about too much anymore [about] what's happening on the other side. You just know, 'OK, if I face this player, they tend to do more [of this].'"</p><p>And things happening automatically is a crucial key to success, in Seider's opinion.</p><p>"The more natural it comes to you, the better off you are," he added. "The game is too fast to be thinking about it for a split-second. Then you're already a second behind. That's something I've definitely learned."</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="AnchorLink" id="image-1d0000" class="Figure-content"><figcaption class="Figure-caption"><p>Red Wings star defenseman Moritz Seider has watched Artyom Levshunov from afar.</p></figcaption><span class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Steph Chambers/Getty Images</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>It's worth noting Seider didn't debut in the NHL until two years after he was drafted, following one full season in the AHL and one in Sweden. Levshunov, on the other hand, debuted nine months after he was drafted. At this point in Levshunov's timeline, Seider was just one month into his Wings career.</p><p>One could argue the Hawks shouldn't have kept Levshunov in the NHL last season, either, but his perceived lack of motivation to play in Rockford might've tied their hands.</p><p>Regardless, his development already seems to be on a more encouraging track this season. He hasn't completely eliminated the glaring mistakes — the "Arty moments" — that plagued him last season, but he has reduced them to only one or two per game.</p><p>Aside from those hiccups, he looks markedly more poised and effective on the ice. He's making smarter decisions, being more predictable to teammates, maintaining better defensive positioning, reading the ice and how plays are unfolding faster and more accurately and skating with the puck more assertively.</p><p>"The more comfortable he gets, he'll get exponentially better," Blashill said. "He's not totally there yet, but he's more comfortable in the systems, he's more comfortable in his skin and he's more comfortable as an NHL player. So it allows him to go out and play and not overthink things."</p><p>Since Bowen Byram's injury, Levshunov leads Hawks defensemen in five-on-five ice time per game, reflecting Blashill's increasing trust.</p><p>And while the other defensemen struggle with defensive-zone exits, Levshunov has been the one guy able to exit semi-consistently. He still sometimes gets in trouble by holding onto the puck too long, but that's preferable at least to making panicked passes that become turnovers.</p><p>Seider, it turns out, has been watching from afar with interest.</p><p>"It looks like the guy doesn't get tired out there," he said. "He's learning the game more and more. It takes a little bit to adjust, but I think his skill level is very underrated. He has great hands in tight areas. Obviously, he's going to be a big part of that blue line for a long time."</p><p>One Seider trait Blashill would like to see Levshunov adopt more is his physicality. Seider uses his size and strength to not only deliver hits but also dominate battles along the boards and separate opponents from the puck. </p><p>Levshunov, being what Blashill calls a "physical freak," has been more physical this season — his hits per game have increased from 1.44 to 1.92 — but he could do even more with that strength.</p><p>"Seider is somebody Arty can look at and say, 'I want to bring that piece to my game,'" Blashill said.</p>

entries.title: Bulls' Caleb Wilson and Matas Buzelis starting to showcase hero mode
entries.summary: <p>This was a glimpse of what it’s supposed to look like.</p><p>What it looked like when they ran together in a South Side summer Pro-Am, late-summer scrimmages, and intra-squad practices.</p><p>Rookie Caleb Wilson doing Caleb Wilson things, both above the rim and on the defensive end. Third-year forward Matas Buzelis trying to win a dunk contest against Knicks players, while continuing to find his three-point stroke that was on the side of a milk carton to start the regular season.</p><p>No, the Bulls didn’t beat the Knicks on Wednesday. A lesson to be learned for another day. But the two foundation pieces – and really the entire starting five – showed up, and Wilson and Buzelis showed out.</p><p>Wilson had 20 points, six rebounds and four assists in the loss to the defending champs, sitting second on the team in scoring with 20.8 points per game. Buzelis had 17 points, five rebounds, three assists and a nifty block, hitting 3-of-6 from three-point range and starting to find his outside rhythm now 5-of-10 the last two contests.</p><p>Who is Batman, which one is Robin? A debate that will eventually play out. Because if this Bulls rebuild is going to move forward like the new front office wants it to they will both need to play hero.</p><p>An idea that continues to bring a smile to Buzelis’ face when he discussed it post-Knicks loss.</p><p>“For sure that felt like the best we’ve showed out so far this season,” Buzelis said. “It’s a new team here and it’s tough. You gotta learn, see where guys are, but we’re slowly building, slowly building. Time will tell, you know, we’re going to be great. We work hard, we try to figure it out every day, and it’s only a matter of time before special comes.”</p><p>That was really displayed in the second quarter on a play in which Wilson delivered a nasty block, got out on the break with the ball, and threw a picture-perfect alley-oop to Buzelis for the slam.</p><p>The same Wilson that played center at North Carolina last season, rarely getting to display such passing talent.</p><p>“In just watching film, figure out where the low man is going to be at, and I feel like I’ve put myself at the top of every scouting report of every team we’re going to play, so just knowing that it is going to attract a lot of gravity and get my teammates open is something I’ve learned to accept and be mature enough to make the right decision,” Wilson said of his sudden ability to play-make. “I’ve been doing that for a minute. It just takes a minute to get calm and adjusted to the NBA. I feel like there’s a lot of things that change throughout the season. My three-point shooting, my ability to create for others, just me getting comfortable. It’s my first year and obviously I have a lot of expectations put on me from other people so I’m just trying to manage that.”</p><p>If that’s “managing” it, yikes.</p><p>Not that Buzelis was surprised. He sees his rookie teammate evolving each day.</p><p>“That’s what I envision us looking like,” Buzelis said. “That’s how you’re supposed to play. That’s what happens when you work hard and try to figure out what you need to do in order to be a successful team.”</p><p>Now can the two replicate that against a Boston team that just ran them out of the Garden at the start of this week? That’s the next test: Going from nail to hammer.</p><p>“Matas is my guy, off the court and on the court, I love playing with him,” Wilson added. “He had a great game (against the Knicks) and I’m excited to see him keep flourishing. I want to connect with him on a bunch more lobs, both ways. I just feel like it’s a step in the right direction. I know Coach (Tiago Splitter) said there’s no moral victories, but I feel like we’re definitely moving the right way.”</p>

entries.title: Patrick Stewart, stage giant also of ‘Star Trek’ and 'X-Men' fame, dies at 86
entries.summary: <p><a class="Link" href="https://apnews.com/article/patrick-stewart-make-so-book-9938aa027c9f6ac0c059417a6e69b9a4" target="_blank" >Patrick Stewart</a>, the classically trained stage actor who scaled the Shakespearean canon and added gravitas to a “Star Trek” franchise and the “X-Men” films, has died. He was 86.</p><p>Stewart died Wednesday in Los Angeles, following “a brief and poignant journey” with Alzheimer's disease and Lewy Body Dementia, spokesperson Kelly Bush Novak said.</p><p>While best known as Professor Charles Xavier and Captain Jean-Luc Picard from the "X-Men" and "Star Trek: The Next Generation" series and films, respectively, Stewart spent more of his career onstage than in the X-Mansion or on the USS Enterprise.</p><p>Besides playing everyone from Claudius to Macbeth, he often performed a one-man rendition of "A Christmas Carol" and did West End and Broadway runs of Harold Pinter's "No Man's Land" and Samuel Beckett's "Waiting for Godot" in repertoire with buddy Ian McKellen.</p><p>He achieved some of the best reviews of his career when he finally tackled Macbeth for the first time. The production, under the direction of Rupert Goold, debuted in May 2007 at England’s Chichester Festival Theatre, switched to London’s West End and then moved to the Brooklyn Academy of Music before transferring to Broadway in 2008.</p><p>Stewart’s performance earned him his sole Tony Award nomination. The Times of London said his Macbeth was “an enthralling creation of frailty, appetite, egotism and grim humor.” The Daily Telegraph said he had turned in “a truly great performance” and The New York Times said it was “a must-see.”</p><p>“Nearly 50 years I’ve waited,” Stewart told The Associated Press in 2008. “I learned it when I was 14. I memorized all the soliloquies just because I thought they were great. And they stuck, so I didn’t have to learn those bits of the play, which is a blessing, because learning lines has now become the one curse of this job.”</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> class="Figure-content"><figcaption class="Figure-caption"><p>Patrick Stewart, left, and Sunny Ozell arrive at the Vanity Fair Oscar Party on Sunday, March 10, 2024.</p></figcaption><span class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Evan Agostini/AP Photo/Evan Agostini</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p></p><h3>Starship commander grew up without a toilet</h3><p>Raised in Mirfield in Yorkshire, a working class corner of northern England, the future 24th century commander of a starship grew up without a bathroom in his house.</p><p>Stewart joined an amateur drama group at 12 and memorized Shakespeare for fun as a teen. He won a scholarship to the Bristol Old Vic Theatre School, launching a career as a character actor.</p><p>He was bald since he was 19 — alopecia runs in his family.</p><p>His father, a former regimental sergeant major in the British Army, was prone to outbursts of “repeated violence against my mother,” as Stewart wrote in a newspaper piece. “Violence is always a choice a man makes and he alone is responsible for it.”</p><p>In his memoir, “Making It So,” Stewart wrote about how he and his older brother Trevor braced for the nights when their dad came home drunk and angry, and attacked their mother. “Sometimes it was with an open hand, other times a closed fist. Always he aimed for her head.”</p><p>The son would later became a patron for Refuge, an organization that provides shelter for domestic abuse victims.</p><h3>Loving Shakespeare proved fruitful as Capt. Picard</h3><p>“The stage would prove to be a safe space, a refuge from real life in which I could inhabit another person, living in another place and time,” he would write.</p><p>Stewart was accepted into the Royal Shakespeare Company and stayed for 14 years, playing everything from Mark Anthony to Henry IV to Shylock to Oberon. “People who were not in the company would say to me, ‘Give it a break. Why don’t you go somewhere else?’ And I would say, ‘To do what?‘” he told the AP. “Telly?”</p><p>Stewart eventually left to look for more varied work, including the 1981 film “Excalibur.” He had just done a production of “Who’s Afraid of Virginia Woolf?” in 1987 when an interesting offer came along. “I found myself in Hollywood shooting a syndicated science fiction series, which I was assured would fail.”</p><p>It didn’t, of course. Thanks to Stewart’s rich baritone and noble bearing, the “Star Trek” franchise ran for seven years, 178 episodes and produced four feature films. He was known for his slogan “Make it so.”</p><p>His adoration for Shakespeare would serve him well when he began to play Jean-Luc Picard, a 24th century starship commander.</p><p>“There is a formality to the way they speak and comport themselves that remind me of numerous Shakespearean situations I’d been in onstage. I should play Jean Luc, I realized, as if he were a character in ‘Henry IV,’ which is about brave men,” Stewart wrote in his memoir.</p><p>Despite the Borg and Klingons, Stewart still managed to make room for blank verse. He established the Paramount Shakespeare Company, a workshop on Saturday and Sunday mornings for any actor interested. (Stewart revisited Picard in the TV series “Star Trek: Picard.”)</p><p>The show gave him a higher visibility, which led to more work, including roles in the films “Conspiracy Theory,” “L.A. Story” and Broadway, where he starred in “The Tempest,” “The Caretaker” and David Mamet’s “A Life in the Theater.” He was knighted by Queen Elizabeth II in June 2010. Stewart was also an ambassador for the International Rescue Committee.</p><h4>A brave and commanding persona. But sexy?</h4><p>In July 1992, he and supermodel Cindy Crawford were on the cover of TV Guide’s “Top Turn-Ons,” based on a readers’ poll. In his memoir, Stewart wrote: “Absurd.”</p><p>Stewart was first introduced as the character Xavier in the original X-Men trilogy, appearing in three films from 2000 to 2006. He later returned in four more movies before Professor X’s death in 2017’s “Logan.” He reappeared in “Doctor Strange in the Multiverse of Madness” in 2022.</p><p>He also showed off his comedic chops aboard Seth MacFarlane’s Starz show “Blunt Talk” for two series and voiced Poop in “The Emoji Movie.” He made appearances on “Robot Chicken,” “Futurama” and “The Simpsons” (in one episode, Homer loses his hair, and Stewart tells him it’s great to be bald.)</p><p>Later in life, he proved Internet-savvy and found new fans with his humor, posing in a bath in a lobster suit and triggering memes when he posted a photo of him picking apples. When he was mistakenly outed as gay by a British newspaper, he said it was a nice change. “At least I didn’t wake up to the internet telling me I was dead again,” he tweeted.</p><p>He married Brooklyn songwriter and singer Sunny Ozell in 2013, with the actor’s “X-Men” co-star McKellen officiating. Stewart later tweeted a photo of the newlyweds in a ball pit.</p><p>He also is survived by two children, a daughter, Sophia, and a son, Daniel.</p>

entries.title: Whole Foods to open shop in Logan Square, replacing former Family Dollar
entries.summary: <p>It will soon be easier for Logan Square residents who don't own a car to shop for grocery essentials at Whole Foods Market, thanks to a development project that will replace the former Family Dollar at Milwaukee and California avenues. </p><p>A date the new grocery, at 2280 N. Milwaukee Ave., will open was not immediately known. </p><p>The smaller-format store will offer a curated selection of groceries and prepared foods in a smaller footprint than a traditional Whole Foods. Located steps from the California Blue Line CTA station, the store could make it easier for commuters and residents to pick up groceries without driving, Ald. Daniel La Spata (1st) said.</p><p>“If we want people needing to make fewer deliveries, people not having to drive as much, being able to walk to a local grocery, being able to step off the train right to a local grocery store – I think it’s a net positive for our neighborhood,” he said.</p><p>La Spata added that the development would not require zoning relief or city subsidies, describing it as a “buy right economic development decision.”</p><p>Whole Foods’ smaller-format stores, known as Whole Foods Market Daily Shop, are designed for urban neighborhoods where shoppers can pick up everyday essentials without navigating a full-size supermarket, according to a company news release in May.</p><p>The company announced a Daily Shop location in Chicago earlier this year at 1200 N. Ashland Ave. in Wicker Park.</p><p>The former Family Dollar property has undergone renovations in recent months, and the store is likely to open on an accelerated timeline, La Spata said. A Whole Foods spokesperson confirmed the development but did not share an opening date or additional operational details with the Sun-Times.</p><p>Logan Square is also slated to get its first Trader Joe’s at 2053 N. Milwaukee Ave., a few blocks away. The store could open next year as the California-based grocer continues to expand in Chicago.</p>

entries.title: Review: Vic Mensa always has Chicago on his mind as he brings ‘Innanetape’ tour back home
entries.summary: <p>Vic Mensa gave one of the defining performances of his career Wednesday night at Garcia’s, resuscitating material that’s 13 years old and proving he was a star from the very beginning.</p><p>The West Loop spot — a 300-seater opened in 2025 as an homage to Jerry Garcia — was an oddball pick for the set and frankly should’ve gone bigger for more to witness. Over the course of the hourlong show, the rapper laid out freshly laundered material from his debut mixtape “Innanetape,” reclaiming its power as a complex genre-leaping tour de force.</p><p> The performance was to mark an album milestone: In September, it finally made its way to streaming services for the first time since it was released in 2013. The move was smart, opening up the album to a whole new generation of fans who may only know Mensa from side hustles with Chance the Rapper, Kanye West and his popular Orange Tree Series on Instagram where Mensa delivers unscripted hot takes from his backyard on politics, history and culture. </p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure It came out the same year as Chance the Rapper's “Acid Rap” and Kanye West’s “Yeezus” and established Mensa as a growing force in the city’s hip-hop scene. XXL<i> </i>magazine even added Mensa to its prestigious Freshman Class for the effort, and giving the album space to come back to life in 2026 feels fitting to re-establish Mensa's importance as he readies a new album for 2027.</p><p>The guest list was telling of this, too. Chance the Rapper was there as the two teamed up for a spitball version of “Suitcase.” It’s a bonus track for the streaming package of “Innanetape” and Wednesday night was just the second occasion they’ve ever performed the song live together (the first was at Metro in 2014).</p><p>Rapper Joey Purp also opened the night, further representing the Savemoney hip-hop collective that also goes way back with Chance and Mensa. Go-to producer and musician Peter Cottontale made an appearance on keys, too. As executive producer of “Innanetape,” he was part of Mensa’s four-piece live band who helped build the rhythmic flow throughout the night. And then there were the star gazers taking it in, like up-and-coming rapper Recoechi and Hilario Dominguez, the much-talked-about candidate running for Chicago School Board president whom Mensa recently endorsed in the Orange Tree Series. </p><p>It wasn’t just out of convenience that Chicago showed up for Mensa — it was out of purpose. The special homecoming gig, part of a four-city Innane Tour, was as much about celebrating the album that made the artist as it was honoring the city and community that shaped him.</p><div class="Figure-content"><figcaption class="Figure-caption"><p>“Anywhere that we’ve gone or anything that we’ve ever done, Chicago has always been top of mind, it’s always been the core, the heart, the nucleus of anything I ever do,” Mensa told the audience during his performance Wednesday at Garcia’s Chicago.</p></figcaption><span class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Candace Dane Chambers/Sun-Times</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>“Anywhere that we’ve gone or anything that we’ve ever done, Chicago has always been top of mind, it’s always been the core, the heart, the nucleus of anything I ever do,” Mensa told the audience. “So if it’s about smacking the s--- out of academics … it’s not necessarily because I hate academics,” he added. “It’s really because I love this place that much. Whatever happens to y’all happens to me.”</p><p>Now based in LA (something prophesied on the “Innanetape” track “Hollywood LA”), Mensa records his new podcast “The Vic Mensa Show” and runs his ORANJ Multimedia Company there. He also spends a lot of time in his paternal homeland of Ghana, helping with humanitarian efforts and cultural projects, not the least of which was the Black Star Line Festival he and Chance launched in 2022.</p><p>But as Mensa confessed in the lyrics of “Didn’t I (Say I Didn’t),” he’s always “got Chicago on my mind.” You could tell by the stories he sandwiched in between the house music-inspired “Down on My Luck” and the heavy riffing of “Tweakin’.” Mensa talked (a lot) about Lollapalooza and the days he was caught making illicit ticket deals on Michigan Avenue. “The thing is with these festivals, many of us from this city, especially on the South and West sides, we’re priced out of that s---,” he said. Mensa also shouted out Kids These Days, the genre-defying high school band he formed with the likes of Macie Stewart, Liam Cunningham (who goes by Liam Kazar now) and Nico Segal. “That music was honestly such a direct precursor to this album because it was so eclectically musical and I had learned so much about jazz and funk and so many different styles that colored and shaped the way [“Innanetape”] came together,” he shared. </p><p>The demise of Kids These Days led to Mensa’s breakout path on “Innanetape,” which he thought up one day while high in his parents’ basement and convinced himself he was the internet. He was out of his mind, sure, but there is a sliver of truth there, at least in the way Mensa’s worldwide connection has played out over the course of his career and in his push for greater global consciousness. This thought pattern was only starting to percolate on “Innanetape” and has continued to evolve as his worldview does.</p><p>The pathway was obvious Wednesday night. When he wasn’t performing music from his debut, Mensa padded in elevated tracks from more recent releases like <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/2021/2/5/22266891/vic-mensa-shelter-new-music-chicago-social-justice-philanthropy" target="_blank" >2021’s “Shelter”</a> about the harrowing experiences of being Black in America and 2017’s solemn hit “We Could Be Free” that ponders the cost of shared human pain.</p><p>These messages are spilling into his newest material, too. Mensa gave space to two new gospel-tinged tracks, “Money Up” and “Rich in Family," which were inspired by his Ghanaian heritage and described as an “anthology through my family history.” The latter song is a particular high mark, with a chorus that proclaims, “all are welcome here … come on in.” </p><p>Mensa’s belief in the power of building community keeps reaching new peaks, but it was first developed here in Chicago’s circles. And that thought didn’t escape him as he wrapped the show with his final words: “I appreciate you for welcoming me back home.”</p><p></p><h3>Vic Mensa set list for Oct. 28, 2026 show at Garcia’s Chicago</h3><p>Orange Soda<br>Hollywood LA<br>Lovely Day<br>Tweakin’<br>Cocoa Butter Kisses (Chance the Rapper cover)<br>Down on My Luck<br>Magic<br>Didn’t I (Say I Didn’t)<br>Money Up<br>Shelter<br>Holy Holy<br>U Mad<br>Suitcase (with Chance the Rapper)<br>Rich in Family<br>We Could Be Free</p>

entries.title: Ald. Nicole Lee wants full-fledged environmental review of Amtrak planned maintenance facility in Bridgeport
entries.summary: <p> Ald. Nicole Lee on Thursday demanded a full-blown environmental review of Amtrak’s proposed maintenance facility in Bridgeport, claiming the assessment promised this week by the Federal Railroad Administration appears to be confined to a dozen local viaducts.</p><p>“I speak on behalf of my community, in that we don’t trust the Federal Railroad Administration to grade its own paper,” Lee said (11th).</p><p>Lee, Cook County Commissioner John Daley and their constituents are embroiled in a high-stakes battle to block Amtrak from moving its maintenance facility from the South Loop to Bridgeport in a move that could set the stage for the White Sox to leave Rate Field.</p><p>Canal Edge LLC — a company owned by White Sox owner-in-waiting Justin Ishbia — has proposed a mixed-use development called <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/white-sox/2026/09/05/new-sox-park-future-owner-announces-proposal-for-riverside-stadium-at-the-railyards" >the Railyards</a> that would move the Sox to the South Loop site currently occupied by Amtrak’s riverfront maintenance facility between Roosevelt Road and 18th Street.</p><p>Ishbia is helping to finance Amtrak’s move to Bridgeport to free up the South Loop site for a new Sox stadium.</p><p>That plan has touched off a <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/white-sox/2026/09/08/justin-ishbia-new-white-sox-stadium-proposal-south-loop-amtrak-railyard-bridgeport-nicole-lee" >political firestorm,</a> in part, because Amtrak received more than $600 million and a “<a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/white-sox/what-to-know-chicago-white-sox-stadium-proposal-justin-ishbia" target="_blank" >categorical exclusion</a>” from the federal government for the project. That allowed Amtrak to move forward without a full environmental assessment or an environmental impact statement “unless there are extraordinary circumstances.”</p><p>Earlier this week, the Federal Railroad Administration (FRA) promised a federal environmental review.</p><p>Lee said the review will give her constituents “a little bit more time, which is good." But the review the FRA promised appears to be confined to a “dozen or so viaducts that would need work between Archer Avenue and 39th Street to help this project move along," she said.</p><p>“That’s how I read it. I’m asking for clarification. And if it is specifically for the viaducts, then it’s even less valuable,” Lee said told the Sun-Times. “If they are not also doing an environmental assessment on the full construction of the project, then we'll proceed with our challenge of their categorical exclusion.”</p><p>Several mayoral candidates — including U.S. Rep. Mike Quigley, retiring Illinois Comptroller Susana Mendoza, Illinois Secretary of State Alexi Giannoulias and lobbyist John Kelly — have joined the fight to block the Amtrak facility.</p><p>But Lee said Mayor Brandon Johnson “has not taken a firm stand in opposition” to the project. The incumbent mayor has simply said the community “deserves answers and needs to be properly engaged,” she said.</p><p>“The city of Chicago absolutely should be behind us… They’re railroading, pun intended, our community to push this through,” Lee said.</p><p>“This is a community that has been very burdened… for many years and decades. How much more are we expected to sacrifice with a 24/7 maintenance operations that’s only going to get busier over time? The whole reason why they want a new facility is because they want increased capacity.”</p><p>At an event hosted by Crain’s Chicago Business in mid-October, Ishbia pitched the proposed Sox stadium in the South Loop as an “amazing opportunity to connect” downtown and the South Loop and “make it one whole downtown community.”</p><p>But Ishbia said the final decision on where the Sox play would be made by Jerry Reindorf, the 90-year-old White Sox chairman whose pitch to build a taxpayer-funded stadium for the Sox at the South Loop parcel known as “the 78” went nowhere.</p><p>Lee is determined to convince Reinsdorf to stay in Bridgeport at a new stadium on the site of Rate Field.</p><p>She’s hoping that a Hail Mary plan to <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears-stadium/2026/10/28/bridgeport-bears-domed-stadium-proposal-sox-rate-field" >build a Bears stadium on the Rate Field site</a> will convince Reinsdorf that state-owned land on 35th Street around the ballpark could be developed into a year-round neighborhood not unlike what the Ricketts family has managed to achieve around Wrigley Field.</p><p>“We know that modern-day sports team owners want things like an entertainment district. They want to have control over those things, and I think that there's a lot that's possible on the site. I'm ready to have the conversation with him,” Lee said.</p><p>“I do think that having the [Bears stadium] proposal… gets lots of people thinking, including Jerry Reinsdorf, about what's possible on the South Side on the current footprint… We want the White Sox to stay right where they are. That would be the biggest win: not to have Amtrak move their maintenance facility and to keep the White Sox. We're gonna continue to do whatever we can to appeal to the Sox to stay and fight with everything that we've got to keep Amtrak out."</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="HtmlModule"><a class="AnchorLink" id="html-embed-module-140000" name="html-embed-module-140000"></a><iframe allow="monetization" frameborder="0" height="200" scrolling="no" src="https://play.prx.org/e?ge=prx_12963_691fc459-c033-4a60-80f7-c50c6379994a&uf=https%3A%2F%2Fpublicfeeds.net%2Ff%2F12963%2Ffeed-rss.xml " style="min-width: 300px;" width="100%"></iframe> </div> </div><p></p>

entries.title: Aurora mayor says $43M flowed from school district to firms linked to indicted board member
entries.summary: <p>Aurora Mayor John Laesch is calling for the resignation of Annette Johnson, an East Aurora School District 131 board member who was indicted this week, accused of orchestrating a lucrative kickback scheme.</p><p>Laesch said he brought prosecutors evidence of more than $43 million in payments to businesses with purported ties to Johnson.</p><p>He previously served on the school board with Johnson, who was the board president and also the chief financial officer of a business at the time of <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/crime/2026/10/27/east-aurora-district-131-board-member-facing-federal-charges-over-fraud-kickback-scheme" >the alleged scheme</a>.</p><p>According to a grand jury indictment Tuesday that charges her with four counts of wire fraud, Johnson used her sway as board president to push the district to buy $2.7 million in wearable air purifiers in 2021 in exchange for a $1.3 million payment to the company that Johnson helped lead.</p><p>Laesch said the “alleged conduct is completely unacceptable, unethical and violates her oath of office.” </p><p>He said a whistleblower approached him in 2024 to report that Johnson purportedly had ties to eight companies. Those companies made $43.1 million from the school district between 2018 and 2023, according to records provided by Laesch.</p><p>The mayor said he provided everything he had to federal investigators and the Kane County sheriff's office.</p><p>“I look forward to seeing this investigation continue and hope for justice for families of District 131 and the East Aurora community,” he said.</p><p>In a written statement, school district officials said: “While the allegations made against Ms. Johnson are incredibly serious and concerning, Ms. Johnson, like all other defendants, is entitled to a presumption of innocence. The district has and will continue to fully cooperate with the authorities in any continued investigation of these matters.”</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="AnchorLink" id="image-1e0000" name="image-1e0000"></a> <picture data-crop="medium"> <source type="image/webp" width="490" height="275" data-srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/b0cde7b/2147483647/strip/true/crop/2400x1347+0+127/resize/490x275!/format/webp/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F79%2F54%2Fe2eb900244e5ab02bbb31864cdfd%2Fforum-abn-040413-4.jpg 1x,https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/a1f4779/2147483647/strip/true/crop/2400x1347+0+127/resize/980x550!/format/webp/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F79%2F54%2Fe2eb900244e5ab02bbb31864cdfd%2Fforum-abn-040413-4.jpg 2x" data-lazy-load="true" srcset="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" /> <source width="490" height="275" data-srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/03f9ed3/2147483647/strip/true/crop/2400x1347+0+127/resize/490x275!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F79%2F54%2Fe2eb900244e5ab02bbb31864cdfd%2Fforum-abn-040413-4.jpg" data-lazy-load="true" srcset="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" /> <img class="Image" alt="Annette Johnson speaks as candidates running for District 131 school board square off during a forum at First Presbyterian Church on Aurora's east side on Tuesday, April 2, 2013. " srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/03f9ed3/2147483647/strip/true/crop/2400x1347+0+127/resize/490x275!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F79%2F54%2Fe2eb900244e5ab02bbb31864cdfd%2Fforum-abn-040413-4.jpg 1x,https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/e3b239c/2147483647/strip/true/crop/2400x1347+0+127/resize/980x550!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F79%2F54%2Fe2eb900244e5ab02bbb31864cdfd%2Fforum-abn-040413-4.jpg 2x" width="490" height="275" data-src="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/03f9ed3/2147483647/strip/true/crop/2400x1347+0+127/resize/490x275!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F79%2F54%2Fe2eb900244e5ab02bbb31864cdfd%2Fforum-abn-040413-4.jpg" data-lazy-load="true" src="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" > </picture> <div class="Figure-content"><figcaption class="Figure-caption"><p>Annette Johnson speaks as candidates running for District 131 school board square off during a forum at First Presbyterian Church on Aurora’s east side in April 2013.</p></figcaption><span class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Jeff Cagle/For the Sun-Times</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>Johnson and her attorney didn’t respond to requests for comment.</p><p>This week’s indictment details a web of dealings and companies, three of them led by Johnson and a romantic partner. That includes the company that allegedly took the $1.3 million payment from a reseller of air purifiers.</p><p>Johnson was involved in purchases and conversations that led to the Nov. 1, 2021, vote approving the $2.7 million purchase, according to the indictment, which said she voted in favor of the deal without disclosing “that she had a personal and economic interest in the sale" and later voted for a $201,000 payment for an “extended warranty” for the air purifiers.</p><p>Johnson’s companies ultimately paid her $7,500 in 2021, though she didn’t list them on her statement of economic interest filed with Kane County, the indictment says.</p><p>Her statements of economic interest were left blank between 2012 and 2024, the year she was accused of having a financial conflict of interest by an Aurora resident who challenged her eligibility for office. The challenge asserted that she had worked for vendors connected to the Elk Grove-based DJ Payne Corporation at least one of which did business with the school district when she was board president.</p><p>The board ruling on the challenge found it didn’t have the authority to challenge the validity of her economic statements and dropped the matter, records show.</p><p>In 2025, a year after the ruling, Johnson listed DJ Payne for the first time in her economic interest statement. The company’s website still lists Johnson as part of its sales team.</p><div class="RelatedList Enhancement" data-module data-align-center> <div class="RelatedList-title">Related</div> <ul class="RelatedList-items"> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/crime/2026/10/27/east-aurora-district-131-board-member-facing-federal-charges-over-fraud-kickback-scheme" >East Aurora District 131 board member facing federal charges over fraud, kickback scheme</a> </li> </ul> </div> <p></p>

entries.title: Pope Leo will vote from the Vatican, by mail, in Illinois' midterm election
entries.summary: <p>He may be the leader of the Catholic church, but Chicago-born Pope Leo XIV is still a registered voter in Illinois and requested a mail ballot for the midterm elections.</p><p>That's according to the Will County clerk's office.</p><p>"Robert Francis Prevost is on the list of individuals who requested a vote by mail ballot for the upcoming election," Kim Fladhammer, Will County clerk's office chief of staff, told the Sun-Times. The pope, who is registered to a New Lenox address, made the request on Oct. 3.</p><p>That mail ballot had to travel a long way — from Joliet to the Vatican City, where Pope Leo has led the Catholic church since <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/religion/2025/05/08/cardinal-robert-prevost-raised-in-dolton-is-the-first-american-pope" target="_blank" >white smoke appeared from the Sistine Chapel</a> in May 2025. </p><p>Records show Prevost voted in the 2012, 2014 and 2016 Republican primaries, as well as in the 2012, 2014, 2018 and 2024 general elections. He also voted in Democratic primaries in 2008 and 2010. He did not vote in Illinois' March primary. In Illinois, voters do not have to register by party and can choose parties for their primary ballot. </p><p>"There is no such thing as an absentee ballot in Illinois law anymore. So anyone can vote by mail if they so choose. There is also a law called UOCAVA, The Uniformed and Overseas Citizens Absentee Voting Act that is mostly for the military, but it's also for U.S. citizens who are overseas," Matt Dietrich, spokesman for the Illinois State Board of Elections said. "...Any Illinois registered voter can vote by mail. Until 2010, it was considered absentee, and you had to have an excuse. But that's all gone away. So that's obviously what he's doing."</p><p>The pope will weigh in on the U.S. Senate race to replace Sen. Dick Durbin and Gov. JB Pritzker's reelection bid, as well as Will County judicial and county races, among other races. </p><p>Pope Leo and President Donald Trump have had some public feuds since the papal leader was elected, including clashes about the war in Iran, immigration enforcement and Venezuela. The pope has been a vocal critic of mass deportations and family separation and has voiced his concerns about the dangers of artificial intelligence and has strongly opposed military strikes and armed conflicts. </p><p>Trump in April <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/pope-leo-xiv/2026/04/13/pope-leo-president-trump-attack-iran-war-chicago-catholics-reaction" target="_blank" >faced backlash</a> for calling the head of the Catholic church “terrible for foreign policy” and posting a since-deleted AI-generated image of the president as Jesus.</p><p>After nearly a year of addressing concern over Trump administration policies, but never name-dropping, Leo directly addressed Trump’s attack aboard the papal plane headed to Algeria, according to the Associated Press.</p><p>“I’m not afraid of the Trump administration or of speaking out loudly about the message of the Gospel, which is what the Church works for,” Leo said.</p><p>Pope Leo returned to the Vatican on Oct. 18, four days after having part of his right lung removed. The surgery confirmed that Leo had lung adenocarcinoma, which is among the most common types of lung cancer. The pope has slowly resumed his public duties, including a weekly general audience in St. Peter's Square. He met with a group of about 30 Chicago clergy, religious leaders and lay people on Wednesday.</p><p>The papal leader, 71, was born in Chicago and grew up in south suburban Dolton. He has seen many Chicagoans visit the Vatican since he became pope, including Pritzker, Mayor Brandon Johnson, Chicago Teachers Union President Stacy Davis-Gates, suburban mayors and even a former member of his favorite baseball team: Chicago White Sox catcher A.J. Pierzynski.</p>

entries.title: Where was Adam Silver when the WNBA needed him?
entries.summary: <p>Thank goodness the Dream forced a Game 7 in San Francisco.</p><p>Had the Valkyries won, the WNBA would have crowned a champion in its 30th season at 2 p.m. on a weekday.</p><p>That’s right, Game 6 was served up as a Thursday matinee because the Dream’s regular 3,500-seat arena couldn’t really fit a Finals game, and an NBA game was scheduled for State Farm Arena Thursday night.</p><p>To resolve the conflict, officials explored moving the dates and venues. Ultimately, they settled on the less-than-ideal solution of hosting a potential clincher before lunch.</p><p>Fans’ outrage prompted finger-pointing. The Dream said they’d raised concerns about the scheduling conflict with the WNBA for months but didn’t receive the proper attention or urgency.</p><p>“Perhaps, our place in the Finals was not accounted for,” the Dream’s ownership group huffed in an open letter to fans.</p><p>On the other hand, multiple reports say that already in December, the WNBA sent a memo to teams with the postseason dates, putting the onus on the teams to resolve any conflicts.</p><p>This happens in sports: The ball drops between two teammates, both having assumed the other would get it.</p><p>Sometimes it’s no big deal. You just move on to the next play.</p><p>But when these miscommunications reoccur, when they happen around the biggest game of the year, it usually signals a need for stronger leadership.</p><p>Hopefully that's coming. Hopefully whoever replaces retiring WNBA Commissioner Cathy Engelbert will have the foresight to resolve these kinds of conflicts. However, that person will still report to NBA Commissioner Adam Silver, and as usual, it’s not clear where he stood on all of this.</p><p>Watching this saga unfold, I thought back to a recent <a class="Link" href="https://www.nytimes.com/athletic/7598169/2026/09/15/adam-silver-wnba-commissioner-hire-unify/" target="_blank" >interview in The Athletic</a>, where he defended the NBA’s control over the WNBA, saying that there are “enormous benefits to running integrated operations.”</p><p>Surely there’s truth to that.</p><p>But in moments like these, when a leader is needed to get NBA teams to be flexible and accommodate the WNBA Finals, isn’t that the <i>exact kind of benefit</i> integrated operations should offer?</p><p>Even if the ball dropping between the WNBA and the Dream put the NBA in an impossible position, how did Silver allow it to get to that point?</p><p>The NBA is an incredibly successful, 80-year-old league that should be advising on how to avoid situations like this.</p><p>I find Silver’s silence on all this very disappointing, if typical for the NBA. The league has never been forthcoming about how it runs its subsidiary, beyond the occasional reminder that they've kept it afloat financially.</p><p>That’s become increasingly grating as the WNBA goes mainstream. Even casual fans want to know how the league is run, and superfans want to properly allocate blame when things go wrong.</p><p>The good news? These Finals show that the WNBA is popular enough to withstand instances of mismanagement. TV viewership broke records, and every Finals game, including the one that started at 11:30 a.m., was packed to the brim.</p><p>Vibes have been immaculate. They should be even better next season.</p><p>The Dream are moving out of Gateway Center and into State Farm Arena permanently, leaving the Mystics as the only WNBA team playing in an arena with fewer than 10,000 seats.</p><p>Maybe in a few years, when every WNBA team has a proper home, fans will laugh about Game 6 being played during brunch. But the NBA’s half-baked stewardship will not be forgotten.</p>
entries.author: Alissa Hirsh

entries.title: Civil rights lawsuit challenges 'inhumane' conditions at Indiana immigration detention center
entries.summary: <p>A coalition of civil rights organizations — including the ACLU, the National Immigrant Justice Center, and the MacArthur Justice Center — filed a class-action lawsuit Thursday challenging the "inhumane and unconstitutionally punitive" treatment of detainees at an Indiana maximum-security correctional facility where many Chicago-area immigrants end up after their arrest.</p><p>A sprawling male prison in Bunker Hill, Miami Correctional Facility, about 150 miles from Chicago, opened around 2001 and today operates for both regular state prisoners and immigration detainees simultaneously. Informally dubbed the “Speedway Slammer” by federal officials, it belongs to a network of more than 250 immigration detention centers nationwide and has increasingly become a regional pipeline for those swept up by federal agents under President Donald Trump’s aggressive deportation policies.</p><p>Civil right attorneys say conditions in the facility have become extremely dangerous, resulting in direct violations of the constitutional rights of detained immigrants. Since 2025, at least two immigrants have died while in custody. They say the lawsuit seeks accountability and the immediate reversal of these harsh conditions.</p><p>“People are suffering, people have died, and more people will suffer and die if those continue,” said Kathleen Hickey, a staff attorney at the ACLU of Illinois filing the lawsuit. “That's why we brought this lawsuit.”</p><p>Neither the Department of Homeland Security nor Indiana officials returned immediate requests for comment about the lawsuit.</p><p>Among the plaintiffs listed in the lawsuit filed in U.S. District Court for the Northern District of Indiana, South Bend Division, is Cynthia Acevedo, a transgender immigrant from Guatemala who has reportedly gone months without consistent epilepsy medication, causing her to suffer multiple severe seizures a week that have resulted in physical injuries, including broken teeth.</p><p>The lawsuit further alleges that Acevedo was the victim of a sexual assault by another detainee after arriving at the Miami Correctional Facility.</p><p>“Defendants failed to take her report on the assault for multiple days (despite her immediate attempts to report it), failed to examine her and conduct a rape kit, failed to provide her medication to prevent transmission of HIV, and failed to provide her requested HIV testing and any test results,” the lawsuit states.</p><p>Hickey says other immigrants have been denied critical HIV medications for months. She and other advocates argue detained individuals are also trapped in a system with dangerously inadequate medical and mental healthcare, exacerbated by filthy living conditions and a lack of adequate food.</p><p>“There's this level of abusive and arbitrary punishments, like solitary confinement, excessive lockdowns, officers using racial and anti-immigrant slurs and excessive use of force,” Hickey said.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="AnchorLink" id="image-ef0000" name="image-ef0000"></a> It also says the agreement was made possible with funds from Trump’s “One Big Beautiful Bill.”</p><p>Civil rights attorneys say local Indiana officials need to be held responsible, too.</p><p>"The state of Indiana and the federal government are working together to create a human rights disaster in one of Indiana's most dangerous prisons," said Alexa Van Brunt, director of the MacArthur Justice Center's Illinois Office. "The conditions are cruel and have resulted in the deaths of innocent people. Both the state and federal government must be held accountable for their heinous treatment of people locked inside Miami.”</p><p>The allegations of harsh treatment at the Miami Correctional Facility aren’t new. Lawyers in this lawsuit also point to a previous legal battle where the ACLU of Indiana recently secured<a class="Link" href="https://www.aclu-in.org/press-releases/aclu-of-indiana-finalizes-1-2-million-in-settlements-over-abuse-at-miami-correctional-facility/" target="_blank" ><u> $1.2 million in settlements </u></a>over inmate abuse at the facility.</p><p>That litigation dates back to 2021, sparked by a single lawsuit filed on behalf of inmate Jeremy Blanchard. That initial case led to dozens of other prisoners coming forward, ultimately resulting in 30 more lawsuits against the Indiana Department of Correction over what plaintiffs described as brutal conditions inside the prison’s "dark cells."</p><p><i>Adriana Cardona-Maguigad covers immigration for WBEZ. Follow her on X </i><a class="Link" href="https://twitter.com/AdrianaCardMag" target="_blank" ><u>@AdrianaCardMag</u></a>.</p>
